Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I am aware of the keen interest which the hon. members of this house have had in the transportation problem of the 1951 grain crop and I thought a brief report on the situation to date would be helpful. The figures which I will put on the record have reference to the period August 1, 1951, to June 12, 1952.
Latest estimates of anticipated marketings from the 1951 crop are 720-4 million bushels. Total marketings from the 1950 crop were 564-6 million. Actual marketings from August 1, 1951, to June 12, 1952, are 619-6 million bushels compared to 479-9 million bushels during the same period in 1950 and 1951 from the 1950 crop. Marketings this season have been greater than at any other similar period in the history of the Canadian grain trade. Car loadings at country points have increased 33 per cent over last year from 221,747 to 295,554 cars.
Total rail and vessel shipments from the lakehead for the present crop year total 370-3 million bushels compared to 223-4 last year, an increase of over 63 per cent.
Shipments to terminals on the Pacific coast this season total 104,947,000 compared to 50,-
970,000	during the same period in the previous crop year, more than a 100 per cent increase over last year.
Total overseas clearances in the same period are 266-3 million bushels compared to 146-5 million bushels from the 1950 crop.
Clearances from the port of Montreal alone since the season opened this year have been particularly large, over 35 million bushels having been shipped compared to 17-7 million for the same period last year, an increase of over 100 per cent. Shipments this season are already greater than at any time in the past in a similar period. Total export clearances from St. Lawrence river terminals since the opening of navigation are 51-4 million as compared to 20-9 million for the same period in 1951.
It should be borne in mind that this last year's crop has been a most difficult one to handle. A seriously delayed harvest last fall, coupled with very poor weather, brought large quantities of out-of-condition grain to market. Salvaging this grain only aggravated an already serious transportation problem. In addition, there has been the problem of getting the immediately saleable grades and types into export channels to meet the excellent demand for our grain abroad.
I think all hon. members will agree that this is a tremendous transportation accomplishment, credit for which should be given in full measure to all the interests concerned, railways, shipping companies, elevator and government employees, not the least of which is the transport controller under whose direction this effort has been achieved.

On the orders of the day:

May I direct another question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) based on the statement he has just made in the house. I am sure that we all appreciate the tremendous efforts which the railway companies have made to move forward the present crop. Has the minister information as to the amount of grain presently in store in country elevators, the estimated amount on farms, and what the weekly loadings are at the country elevators? We would then have some idea of what the position might be on July 30.

speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister in connection with the present position of the commission on the South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project. Have any interim recommendations been made? When is a report expected, and is any consideration going to be given to that report in so far as early commencement of the work during the present session is concerned?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Earlier this morning the hon. member was kind enough to send to my office a notice of his intention to ask this question. The only answer I can make at this time is that for the last three months or more the work has been prosecuted very vigorously by the commission. About the middle of April the secretary of the commission reported orally and then confirmed in writing to the Acting Prime Minister that the commission had found it necessary to retain the firm of Mannix Limited of Calgary to prepare an estimate of the owners' cost of the project. On June 6 I received from the secretary a letter informing me that this would mean an increase over the previous estimate in the expenditures the commission would incur in performing its duties. For that reason in the supplementary estimates that have been tabled a supplementary item has been included in order to cover that additional expenditure. There has been no other recommendation than the one for the money necessary to cover what the commissioners considered it was necessary to do. There have been no other recommendations about it to date.
I know that the commission realizes the government's anxiety to get the report at the earliest possible date. From conversations I know that the commissioners are doing their best to meet that desire. I should not like to fix a date. They have not been able to tell me just exactly when their work will be completed. I can say that it will not be within the next few days, and there will not be an opportunity of receiving or of communicating their report to members of parliament just at this time. I can assure the hon. member that we realize that not only the public of Saskatchewan but the public generally do not like to see unexplained delays in the performance of these tasks that are considered 
of general public interest. The commissioners fully realize that fact, just as we do. The best efforts will be put forward to avoid any justifiable criticism in that regard.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Did I understand from the Prime Minister that the report is expected? I understood that the commission contemplated the holding of public hearings in the province of Saskatchewan. Are those public hearings to be undertaken, and are they to commence soon?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION

Everything is proceeding as fast as it can be done. I am sure that if the government of Saskatchewan felt that public hearings were not absolutely necessary and that they might be apt to occasion delay, they would waive that matter.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION

view of the fact that the Old Age Security Act came into effect on January 1 of this year, is it the intention of the government to continue in force the earlier Old Age Pensions Act under which the provincial governments are now called upon to collect claims against many thousands of pensioners' estates, some of which would, of course, have arisen just a day or so before the new act came into effect?

I thank the hon. gentleman for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. As he knows, the Old Age Pensions Act was a co-operative measure in which the provinces as well as the dominion government paid contributions, the dominion government to a substantial extent.
The government has written to all of the provinces asking whether, from their point of view, there is any objection to the repeal of the Old Age Pensions Act. We are informed that no orders have been placed for Holland strawberries by Montreal or Quebec jam makers, but that with an abundant crop in sight processors are buying at 10 cents a pound, with some purchases as low as 8 cents. Belleville Harbour Commissioners Speaker, I do not think that this bill will be found controversial but perhaps a short statement would be in order. speechtext: SO. To provide capital assistance for the construction, acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works by private contractors engaged in defence contracts, or by crown plants operated on a management-fee basis, or by crown companies under direction of the Minister of Defence Production, subject to approval of treasury board, $85,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three questions I should like to ask the minister with regard to this item which is for $85 million. The general purpose as I understand it is to provide assistance to war industry and I notice that in the supplementary estimates there is what appears to be a further vote of $25 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is correct.

That would make a total of $110 million.
My first question is this: Has any consideration been given by the department to using some of this money to assist in bringing to Canada industry which would be useful for defence production and which we do not have in the country at the present time? There must be specialized industry in Great Britain and on the continent which could be of great help if it were to become established here in Canada, and I am wondering whether the vote is wide enough to give the department power to make expenditures for that purpose, and whether the government has any policy along that line.
It always seems to me so perfectly clear that if conditions are as bad as we believe them to be, and if they should finally result in a third world war, then the industries in Great Britain particularly and also those on the continent would be subject to atomic attack; and it would be very, very difficult for them to carry on their production. Just

as a matter of safety there seems to be a good deal of merit in transplanting as many key industries as possible to this continent.
I do not intend to go into the matter further but I would ask the minister if he would deal with this question. I have one or two other questions as well.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is the policy to bring firms from the continent, and particularly from the United Kingdom, to Canada provided their production is needed in the defence program. The vote is not wide enough to bring a firm to Canada and provide capital assistance if the company has no place in the defence program. If the full production of a new plant in Canada is required for war production we bring it- and we have brought several plants here. One is the Sperry plant which makes a special line of instruments never before made in Canada. SKF make special roller bearings used in aircraft work. Lucas Rotax of the United Kingdom make fuel systems not only for aircraft built in Canada but also for aircraft built in the United States. That is a big industry. Steel Improvement makes blades for the turbines in airplane jet engines. Peacock Brothers make special equipment used in the naval escort vessel program. One very large capital expenditure is being made to expand the turbine production of English Electric. We had a small turbine production here in Canada and that is to be expanded very considerably. The turbine designed by English Electric in the United Kingdom is to be built here in quantities sufficient to supply the turbines for the escort vessel program.
Those are the examples that occur to me at the moment but I would say there is no provision in this vote to bring English talent or continental talent if the facility is not required for defence work.
But it can be done under this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. My hon. friend will understand that all property acquired under this vote is property of the crown. New arrangements would have to be entered into if the present operator wishes to continue on a peacetime basis. The equipment is installed for war production only and rental agreements or purchase agreements would be necessary if the occupant wishes to use the same equipment for peacetime production.

I take it there would not be a great deal of difficulty in working out some arrangement that would allow these firms to carry on in peacetime.
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No. We try to get the best competitive prices but we also try to work out an arrangement with the occupant of the plant if he gives an indication that he can carry on successfully in peacetime.

What part does the Department of Defence Production play in deciding whether or not a firm shall qualify for depreciation? I realize there must be great difficulties in working out a fair plan to follow out the policy, but I have had some suggestions from the west coast that the time has now come to widen the power for taking depreciation. Apparently some of the smaller firms find that they are not able to qualify for the depreciation, and it may be that we are now in a position where some provision should be made for firms which, to date, have not qualified for such depreciation. Will the minister tell us what the situation is in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, the issuance of certificates providing for deferred depreciation is administered by the Department of Trade and Commerce, but probably that does not matter so far as this discussion is concerned. The regulations governing the issuing of certificates are fairly well outlined by the orders in council which have been tabled. There are certain types of production that are regarded as essential which automatically qualify a firm for the depreciation allowance. Then there are others that can qualify if they are essential to the defence effort; that is a qualification for the judgment of the minister. Some latitude is allowed in the case of a plant that can contribute, even indirectly, to the defence effort.
The list of conditions providing approval has been broadened from time to time, and I believe we are getting near a point where consideration can be given to repealing that legislation or at least rendering it inoperative. The situation has been recently made uncertain by the steel strike. The purpose of the regulations was twofold: first, to check the building boom which was contributing to inflation, and second, to conserve materials for the defence effort. Probably the first objective is no longer as important as it was at the time the regulations were issued, but the second objective becomes more important as a result of the stoppage of steel supplies from the United States. We shall have to re-assess the effect of the steel strike before we can arrive at a termination date.
I believe that at this time a termination of the regulations is indicated rather than a further relaxation. It would be difficult to be fair if the regulations are relaxed further. Within the limits of the regulations now, we can have an administrative staff that can

Supply-Defence Production establish a sharp dividing line between projects that qualify and projects that do not qualify. If the regulations were broadened it would be difficult to find that sharp dividing line.
The minister thinks that once the steel strike is settled, it might be possible to remove the restriction altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would not like to indicate that that could be done immediately. I say that after the strike is over we can assess the supply situation, and probably determine a date at which the regulation would be removed. I would expect that termination date would be a few months subsequent to arriving at the decision.

The situation was put very clearly by one of my correspondents. He said:
. . . we feel the restrictions should be released to give all industry an opportunity to purchase capital equipment to keep their plants up to date and modernize their operations so they will be in a position to be at their best as far as manufacturing is concerned, in preparation for any eventuality which might come along.
I think that this particular firm-I have no doubt others are in the same position- is finding it difficult to keep equipment up to date because the depreciation is deferred. I would hope it would be possible fairly soon to do away with these restrictions.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I might point out that the penalty for not being able to write off depreciation immediately is not severe so far as equipment is concerned. A firm loses nothing in the long run because the equipment is eventually all written off. Nevertheless, as I have said, consideration will be given later in this year to removing the provision.

I am interested in the statement of the minister respecting the encouragement to the introduction into Canada of industries that have been established in Great Britain and the countries of continental Europe. He has named a number of such industries, and it would appear to me that those industries represent a considerable amount of capital and employment, having regard to the volume of materials required in those industries. I would point out to the minister the special claim of the maritimes with respect to the establishment of new industries of this kind. The maritime provinces, and especially Nova Scotia, have not fared well in this respect in either of the wars-in fact, since confederation. Many of our native industries have been transferred to central Canada and in recent years we have suffered greatly from a lack of industry.
fMr. Howe.J

I recognize that the minister has given some encouragement to the establishment of defence industries in that part of Canada within the last few years. He has always expressed a willingness to expand that policy. I want to make an appeal again to the minister for special consideration by his department with respect to the establishment of such industries in the maritime provinces. If the minister has some statement that would be of interest to that part of Canada, I think it would be quite appropriate for him to make it now and I would be greatly interested in any statement relating to the transfer of industries from Great Britain or continental Europe to the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, an effort is made to distribute capital assistance as widely as possible across Canada. I believe we have had some success in the maritime provinces. I have not a list before me at the moment, but Fairey Aviation of Canada has been established substantially through capital assistance. Employment in the plant is expanding. Cossor (Canada) Limited have had capital assistance in establishing themselves in Halifax, and that is an industry that was transported from England. It is thriving in the maritime provinces. In the town of Amherst, which my friend knows something about, substantial capital assistance has been given to Enamel and Heating Products Limited, to allow them to make aircraft components on a large scale which will give employment to people of the area. The Trenton Steel Works has been assisted to the extent of $2-9 million. That is for the production of rotor forgings for our shipbuilding program. The Saint John Drydock has been given substantial capital assistance. There are other firms, and I am sorry that I did not bring a list, but I think the hon. member will find that if there is any firm in the maritimes that is ambitious to undertake a defence contract, every encouragement will be given and capital assistance granted, if that is indicated as a requirement.

There is one matter I should like the minister to clear up for me, if he can. It is in connection with aircraft production, especially as related to T-33A. I noticed from the evidence given in the special committee that in the United States these aircraft cost about $93,500, and yet when we build them in Canada they cost us $277,000. It would seem to me that in most instances where we are building these in Canada, it is costing us about $115 million. If that is not correct I wish the minister would give an explanation of it, because it seems a pretty serious procedure to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is very difficult to assess costs against aircraft. The tooling up has to be charged against the first quantity, and the costs then come down substantially. The costs here are shown as pre-production, $50,000; production costs, $90,648,000; tooling costs, $10,643,000; royalties $2,137,000. Then there is about $15 million more for spares and ground handling equipment. The cost per aircraft will depend entirely on the number that are required. At the moment we have an order from the R.C.A.F. It was not possible to purchase the planes outside Canada. They just were not available, and therefore to carry out our duties for procurement we are tooling up to manufacture the aircraft. If we can write the tooling costs off against twice the number of planes now on order the costs per plane will decrease. My information is that in another contract that Canada has for the Sabre aircraft our manufacturing costs in Canada are slightly lower than the manufacturing costs in the United States. I think probably when the final accounting is made on the T-33, it will show the same results.

May I add one more sentence? Mr. Drury said:
Our known requirements at the moment do not extend beyond this figure of 576 for the three-year program.
I would take it from that there will not be any more of these planes built. It seems to me that we would be better off to go to the United States and buy these. I suggest that they could save money. The sum of $115 million is a fantastic amount to pay simply so that the planes may be made in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I would agree that we might be better off to go and buy them in the United States but there is an "if" there: if we could buy them. But we have information that the production capacity in the United States is fully booked for the foreseeable duration. Mr. Drury states the Canadian requirement. In almost every case of Canadian production there is a subsequent requirement from elsewhere tacked on to the Canadian production. For example, we have the Canadian production of Sabres; we also have production for the United Kingdom of Sabres and we also have the United States requirements for Sabres manufactured in Canada. It is very difficult to theorize about the production of aircraft because development of programs change the situation very materially. What looks to be an expensive aircraft at one stage turns out to be a low-cost aircraft at another stage, owing to the fact that the pre-production costs and the tooling costs are spread over a greater number of aircraft, and that the improving skills
Supply-Defence Production of the workers bring down the cost of producing subsequent aircraft.
If at some time my hon. friend is interested I shall show him a typical production curve which discloses a very sharp drop during the production of the first 100 aircraft and a decelerating drop carrying on throughout the length of the contract. Unless you can foresee at what point on the curve the production will be terminated, it is impossible to give an accurate forecast of the cost of the aircraft.
My hon. friend wants to close off at the Canadian requirements and say, that is it, that is what we are going to charge Canada, then it would be cheaper if we could buy them somewhere else. I would agree in theory, but I am not prepared to take that under the circumstances. Our experience is that if we have aircraft in production there is always a market for them during the defence build-up.
Have we been able to get the engines?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, we have the engines.
Up until recently it was difficult?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We are only scheduling the building of aircraft to meet the availability of engines, but for the T-33 we are using a British engine which is in relatively good supply.

The minister, I think, is quite certain that we are going right into a war; at least we are getting ready to go into a war. In connection with providing for Canada's defence needs in case of war, while sugar supply is just a little off the beaten path, I think it is fitting that we bring it up here. The minister remembers something about our sugar difficulties during the last war. He remembers that instead of expanding our production of beet sugar, which we neglected to do, we had to depend on outside sources. The result was that sugar was rigidly rationed considerably below the ration allowed in the United States during the war.
It looks to me as though in all the fine things the minister is saying about defence industries he is making no provision for an adequate supply of sugar for the Canadian people if we cannot get that sugar from abroad. In case war breaks out no one can possibly foresee the difficulty which will be encountered. Any ships that we get from outside Canada will be carrying other things. The bottoms that we would ordinarily use to firing sugar into the country will be used for other purposes. All these considerations, it seems to me, should indicate to us the wisdom of making adequate provision for the production of our own sugar. It would not

Supply-Defence Production take any more than probably $50 million wisely invested all across Canada, in the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario and the prairie provinces, where beet sugar can be produced, to provide the factories to produce the sugar that will be needed during the next war, rendering us secure.
It may be argued that we shall not have any need for this productive capacity after the war, but I would say that we shall have much more need for that kind of production after the war than we shall have for the type of production that is being envisaged in the factories that we are building for aircraft and other munitions of war. I am just wondering whether or not the minister has given attention to the advisability of expanding Canada's beet sugar production facilities to meet possible needs such as I have indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: While Canada is not selfsufficient in sugar, the British empire is selfsufficient in sugar. I cannot think of any worse calamity to the West Indies than for Canada to produce all her sugar requirements from beet sugar. The West Indies are dependent on this market. The market has been open to them and was open to them during the second world war. While we did have to be a little careful-perhaps it would be good for most of us to be a little careful about the amount of sugar we take-the Canadian food supply has not been seriously crippled by lack of sugar. Canada is a trading nation, and I think we should avoid trying to become self-sufficient in anything just for the sake of doing that. I think we should produce those things that we can produce most economically and furnish a market to other allied countries for the things that they produce in surplus, hoping that they will continue to furnish a market for the things that Canada produces in surplus. Of all the countries of the world Canada is in the least danger of being crippled in the matter of food supply, and I think it would be unwise to spend any part of this vote for stepping up Canada's food supply.

I appreciate the minister's position. It is the orthodox one that was told me fifteen years ago. I believe it is fallacious, nevertheless, and I will tell the minister why. It was not very long ago that he gave a talk in Montreal in which I thought he displayed much wisdom. In that talk he said we were endeavouring to decrease our vulnerability as a nation. That must mean that Canada is getting more and more to the point where she is able to produce what she needs. What other meaning could the minister have in mind in using the word "vulnerability"? While Canada is safe in the main in respect of food, the one important
[Mr. Blackmore.1

food in which she is not safe in the event of a serious turn in the world situation is this very item of sugar. For Canada to be vulnerable in respect of sugar is utterably fantastic when you consider the fact that Canada can economically produce sugar in large quantities in so many areas of the Dominion of Canada.
There is another respect in which I think the minister should qualify his position; it is this: He speaks of our keeping ourselves free from producing sugar in order that we may provide a market for some other countries. That is a fine, altruistic attitude to take, but it just happens that we do not take that attitude with respect to any other commodity than sugar, as far as I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, yes; we do.

I would be interested to be instructed. But as far as I know sugar is the only food which we can easily produce and which we do not produce in adequate quantity to supply our own needs in case of war. That state of affairs requires quite a good deal of justification.
There is one more aspect to this thing. We are rapidly getting to the point-and I am sure the minister, with the breadth of vision that he has, sees that the time is coming when this will be the situation-when there are not going to be enough external markets for the production of goods in the Americas. No matter how we try to find external markets enough, we are not going to be able to do so. We must have some other means of distributing the production of this continent into the hands of the needy people through the world; by that I mean some other method than the one we have been using up to the present time. I am not going to go into details as to how that is to be done, but it must be done. If men like the minister are not thinking about how to do it, probably they will wish they had done so, and so will the people who are relying on them with such complete confidence as we are relying on the minister at the present time. We simply must find a way of getting the surplus production from America into the hands of the 1,500 million people who are obliged to go to bed hungry every night. When a means of that kind is discovered, it will not be at all difficult to distribute the sugar which is produced by the British commonwealth. Until a means of distribution such as the one I have indicated is discovered, there will be difficulty for everybody to find markets-in the British commonwealth as well as in the United States.
I do not think that the minister's argument there is particularly valid; I do not think it is nearly as valid as are most of his arguments. I still maintain that we would be well advised

to make provision now, before we get into too many difficulties, for the production of at least all the sugar that Canada needs.
There is one more little aspect to this thing which is extremely important. As the minister knows, while the war was on we were told that we could not increase the ration of sugar for Canadians because we needed the sugar for various military purposes. The minister knows those military purposes quite as well as I do, or better. Those military needs for sugar were exceedingly urgent. They were extremely important. Why not have all of our sugar produced in Canada so as to assist in supplying our military sugar requirements? I think that is an argument which will appeal to the minister, as he thinks it over. So I say once more in this chamber, just as I said many times before world war II: Let us get ourselves ready to produce our own sugar. It will be a blessing to us from every standpoint and it can do us no harm whatsoever.
Oh, yes.
One hon. member says "Oh, yes". I shall be glad to take the hon. member on in a debate on this subject.
How will our friends get Canadian dollars to buy our products?

If I caught the hon. member's question correctly, he asks what the difficulty is. May I point out that one year it cost 28 million United States dollars to buy our sugar. I think my hon. friend will recognize that that is a serious item. If there is any one really serious anxiety to Canada, it is the danger of an adverse trade balance with the United States. Nearly every bit of sugar we buy from abroad works down to United States dollars in one way or another.
How?

A great deal of it is brought from areas that require United States dollars. The important thing is for the hon. member to read up on the subject and to come back here; then I will debate with him on this subject. I maintain that there is no single line of development economically in Canada that will be more in the interests of Canada than the development of the beet sugar industry all across this country.

Has the minister checked the situation with regard to the manufacture of electronics on the west coast? Apparently about two weeks ago an eastern firm by the name of Canadian Aviation Electronics Limited announced, with quite a big splash, in Vancouver, that they would be providing all the electronic radar needs for west coast defence. There are already several firms
Supply-Defence Production there which I believe are well able to do this type of work. They resent this other firm walking in, presumably with the contracts. I do not know what the actual picture is; but perhaps the minister can tell the committee just what has happened there.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: With regard to the firm mentioned, no order has been given for production on the west coast. I am told that the firm denied that they made the statement that was quoted in the paper. I read the first announcement with somewhat of a shock. There are several firms on the west coast which made a fine contribution in electronics in the last war. Those firms are being used in the present defence effort. The trouble with the electronic program has been that considerable time is required for design and development before equipment can be put into production. That program is really just coming into production now. I think that firms on the west coast which are capable of doing that work can look forward to the same sort of treatment which they received in the last war which I think they found to be quite satisfactory.

When the defence estimates were before the committee on the last occasion, the minister was good enough to arrange for the deposit of the contracts which were discussed that evening. Among those contracts was one with Avro, and with regard to that contract I want to ask some questions. The contract actually was considerably earlier in date than, I think, the other contracts which were deposited. However, I do not know that we need to go into that matter. Actually I think the contract was made before the passing of the Defence Production Act. But again, as I say, I do not think I need to labour that point. What I want to do in general is to ask the minister some questions about the financing of Avro-that is A. V. Roe (Canada) Limited- and also to ask him some questions about the production.
First of all, my general objective is to find out how much public money has gone into Avro; how much, if any, private money has gone in, and the results achieved. One of the motives in working up the Avro enterprise was, I think, a natural and proper motive, namely doing our own construction here. Mr. Deisher, vice president and general manager of A. V. Roe Limited, speaking in February, 1946, said this:
We are going to build aircraft designed to suit Canadian conditions. Canada has always built the other fellow's product. Now we are going to have aircraft that are Canadian from the drafting board to the stars.
Here are my questions. The first question I should like to ask is this. What were the
3620	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production arrangements with Avro in 1945 when the government made available the real estate, buildings and equipment previously controlled by Victory Aircraft? That is my understanding of the first transaction. I suppose it can be worked out in terms of investment. There must have been a figure at that time. Will the minister answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
At the close of the war we were able to sell the Canadair plant to private interests and we were anxious to do something with Avro. The government was hardly in a position to enter into competitive aircraft manufacturing. The plant was called Victory Aircraft in those days. The Avro interests came out from England to discuss the matter and after a good deal of discussion we decided to let them operate the Victory plant on a temporary basis to see whether they could make a success of it.
An arrangement was entered into in 1945 that they would take over the management of the plant at a rental of 50 per cent of the profits on the operation. There was the usual peacetime amount of aircraft repair work to be carried out. At the same time we asked them to take over the work that the government had been doing in the development of a jet engine. The production of the jet engine was financed at the Avro plant. There were also supplies in the plant which had to be liquidated, and Avro took over that responsibility for government account. That arrangement carried on until 1948 and I think a modest profit was made in each year, 50 per cent of which was paid to the government as rental.
By 1948 the work in the plant had been liquidated; that is, the government stocks in the plant had been liquidated and we entered into negotiations with Avro to purchase the plant. The result was that the plant was purchased by Avro at a sum close to $2 million, which was paid in cash.
Then in 1949 the R.C.A.F. through the Minister of National Defence came forward with a proposal to undertake the design of a long-range, twin-engine, all-weather fighter, and of the jet engine to power the fighter. It was the wish of the R.C.A.F. that Canada be independent as far as the defence of Canada in the air was concerned. It was felt that there was no existing aeroplane suitable to meet Canadian requirements, which was the coverage of long distances without refuelling. Therefore that work was assigned to A. V. Roe and has been carried out by them subsequently. The engine and the aircraft are now coming into volume production.

As I understand it, from 1945 until 1948 A. V. Roe was on a kind of agency-rental basis under which


they paid rent out of the earnings. Then in 1948 they paid $2 million cash. How much was the government investment at that time? Presumably there would be a figure on your books indicating that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It was about $6 million. The plant was bought for $2 million. My hon. friend will appreciate that a special purpose plant cannot be sold for the full value when there is no work in sight to justify the investment of $6 million. It must be sold at a discount. We were anxious to bring some United Kingdom designing experts in to Canada and it was decided that it would be good business for the government to sell that plant to Avro for $2 million.
What advances have Avro had since that time? One hears various figures, some of which I am sure are exaggerated, but there must be a specific figure of the total advances up to the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Since Avro has been the agent of the government to build an engine plant there has been an authorized expenditure of $37,797,000 to date. That engine plant is separate from the A.V. Roe property, as my hon. friend probably knows. It is in Malton, but in a different area. That engine plant is wholly owned by the government. Expenditures have been authorized to the extent of $5,580,000 for the expansion of the aircraft facilities at the old plant that Avro own. Pre-production expenses at the present time stand at $35,492,050 and total capital pre-production and development $104,277,600.
Does that include the $37 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, that is the authorized expenditure for buildings and tools bought for government account and owned by the government; that is capital included in this vote.
That is on the aircraft, not on the engine?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Both.

Let me see
if I have these figures right. There was the original amount of $37 million. What is the operating arrangement in connection with that As I understand it, the government set up this plant and Avro was to operate it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That contract has not been finalized. There will be a fee paid to Avro for operating the plant, but it has not been worked out as yet.
When was the plant begun?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It was begun about the summer of 1950 and is just being completed.

Let me see
if I have these figures correct. The first figure I have is $37 million; then there is a figure of $5 million; then there was the pre-production figure of $12 million, making a total of $54 million. Then I understood the minister added $73 million, which would give a total of $127 million. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; I think I can straighten it out. Capital investment to date is $27,163,200; development expenses for both engine and aircraft, $41,622,350; pre-production expenses, $35,492,050. There is a figure here of $17,182,000 for production of aircraft and spares. Total payments to date amount to $121,459,700.
I gather from the minister that apart from the actual expenditure payments there are certain authorizations outstanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I gave the authorization for capital account and I also gave the expenditures for capital account. The difference of about $12 million represents certain development work that was not paid for when these figures were compiled.
So the expenditure up to the moment is roughly $120 million. Does that include the figure of $16 million which the minister gave us in the committee on May 30?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What was the $16 million for?

At page 2783 of Hansard for May 30 the minister said:
This year the vote is $85 million, which includes a carry-over of $66 million from last year. That is allocated as follows . . .
Then among the various companies there is an amount of $16,176,000 for the A. V. Roe jet engine plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It does not include that. That was a forecast of capital expenditures for the new year. That has not been authorized yet. It is subject to review and it probably will be cut down materially.
But something of that $16 million should be added to the $120 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

Do these figures include the whole of the amount mentioned in the letter of August 18, 1950, which amended the original contract of May 9, 1949, and which increased the original amount from $6,450,000 to $19,876,000? Is that figure of $19,876,000, which is included in the letter of August 18, 1950, included in this $130 million?
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It has been included to the extent that the money has been spent. I gave my hon. friend all the money that has been paid to A. V. Roe for every purpose up to date.
I just wanted to be sure that it covered that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is difficult to sort out the bits and pieces here but I have tried to give the over-all figure.

I am interested in that figure. As a matter of fact it is twice as much as I thought. I want to find out something about production. I understand that originally the plant had two or three objectives. One was the Chinook engine which, for reasons we need not go into, was not proceeded with. Then there was the jet liner and the Orenda engine. I am interested in the Orenda engine. There were some flowery speeches made about it although not by the minister. He did not make any flowery speeches but some were made and I should now like to get some facts. When did the Orenda make its first test flight? First let me read an extract from the letter of August 18, 1950, addressed to the A. V. Roe company and signed by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. It reads as follows:
It is contemplated that the additional capital expenditure authorized by this letter-
That is the amount to which I previously referred.
-will permit the following increases in production but no authorization in respect to production is given in this letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I should like to point out to my hon. friend that that letter is marked "secret". It got into the file by mistake but there is no need to read it in parliament.
*

There is
nothing I want to do less than to read a secret letter. I got it along with the contracts. Actually, with deference to the minister, I would not have thought this information was very secret but if the minister wants me to stop reading the letter I am agreeable.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would prefer that it should not go on Hansard.
Then I will ask my next question. When did the Orenda make its first test flight?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is difficult to say. The engine ran for a thousand hours or more in static tests and then was put in what is called a flying test bed. In other words, it was put in a Lancaster plane that had two internal combustion engines. It was flown there and finally was put in a commercial aircraft and flown about a year ago, I believe. I went to

Supply-Defence Production Toronto to see the first CF-100 powered with an Orenda engine fly about a year ago.

I am
informed that there were tests as far back as January, 1950. Am I wrongly informed?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The static testing of the engine or type testing was completed in 1950. The bringing of an engine into being from zero is a very lengthy process. If my hon. friend were to compare it with anybody else's engine from zero to full production he would find that it compares very favourably. If you try to get the story of this engine by itself it sounds like a long time, and I may say that it sounds like a long time to me.
I can believe that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: However, if I look up the record of any other engine I find that the time is about the same.

I am not setting myself up as an expert. I am merely asking questions. I realize what the minister says is true, that it does take a long time, but there is such a thing as a long time being too long. Again I am only asking questions. When was the first actual order placed?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We were expecting to be examined on capital assistance. If we had expected to be examined on production we would have brought different documents. I am afraid I cannot give that information, but when you are moving from development into production contracts are not very important. You place a production contract when you are sure you are in production but before that you are working on development. I do not remember when the first production contract was made. I have something here with respect to ten pre-production aircraft but that is not a production contract.

I do not want to be un-co-operative but I am very anxious to get this information. I was interested in the minister's statement a moment ago when he said he was inclined to think it was a rather long time. I have forgotten his exact words. I am very anxious to know exactly what the time involved was. I have certain questions with regard to the contract and production situation and if the minister has not the figures I would suggest that this item might stand. There are other items with which we could proceed. I do want these figures and I think we should have them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I may say in general that we are now in production although it is true we are not up to capacity. We are producing a


commercial Orenda engine and we expect to be up to capacity by the end of the present calendar year. There is every indication that when we are at capacity the cost of the engine, including all development and preproduction costs, will compare with engines of the same thrust.
There is an active demand for this engine. We need it ourselves. We would like to power the Sabre with it and we intend to do'so. When we can do that we will have a much better aircraft than the one we are producing now because the Orenda is more powerful than the American engines we are now putting in the Sabre aircraft. We also require Orendas to match the production of the Canuck, the airplane for which the engine was developed.
We believe we have a very useful engine. Our pre-production costs are not out of line we find, and everything indicates that the price of the engine will be in parallel with competitive engines and that the operation will develop into a profitable operation.
If my hon. friend wants to go into a complicated subject such as this is-and I am sure that no one else in the house does- then if he will sit down with our accountants I am sure we can go through it and check each stage. I cannot do that here. I sit down with my accountants and try to get the thing in my mind and to keep the situation in focus, but there is a great mass of detail and I do not think he can get the information that he wants by questioning me. I am sure that he cannot because I do not know all the answers. There is a very considerable amount of detail when you produce an airplane and an engine and go through the development, testing, pre-production, and tooling stages.

I am very interested in what the minister says and although he does not know it he is making me more and more anxious to get some of these facts. I do not think he suggests that there is any difficulty in getting the answer to my question. It was: When was the first order actually placed? I want those figures and I suggest that the item stand until three o'clock. I want the figures and I have been surprised and interested in the figures we have received already.
I had in mind, after making the best inquiries I could, as I have said earlier this morning, the figure of $120 million, very different from which the minister gave us earlier. I had a figure about half that in my mind which was all I had been able to get up to the moment. I am interested in these figures and I am equally interested in the

figures on production. I am grateful too for the information we have had.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I might point out to my hon. friend that he is talking about an engine made in a government plant for government account. Everything in that engine plant has been done for a government account. I do not know why he is anxious to know when the order was placed. I suppose we would give a contract to a privately owned plant if the work were performed there-but he is talking about Orenda engines built in a government-owned plant with which no one but the government is concerned.

I am rather surprised at the minister's last comment- that he does not know why I want to ask these questions. If I am the only one who is interested it is too bad. There are a lot of people who ought to be interested and I think this is a matter of importance. We should know what we have received for over $120 million. I accept the general statement that the minister has made that it takes a long time to produce a new type of engine. We have had very flattering references to this engine but I am just asking for simple facts. When did we give the first contract? What has happened since, and so on? Those are very simple questions which I am sure the department can answer and I suggest to the minister that I am not asking anything unreasonable when I ask to have answers to those questions. I suggest that the item stand until three o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have no objection to that but I might point out that the questions asked have nothing to do with the item. The item is capital expenditure. I am prepared to give you every fact about capital expenditure but my hon. friend is asking about production figures and there is nothing in this vote that covers production. Production is paid for by national defence and they are the proper people to ask about production figures.

The minister surprises me doubly. I would have thought if I had asked national defence, they would have said: Ask defence production, they are looking after the carrying out of the contracts. I am also surprised that the minister should say that we should not be interested in what we are getting for our money. The minister in effect says that we should not ask that, or that if we should ask we should ask someone else. I find that a very great surprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Life is full of surprises.
Supply-Defence Production

I am interested and I hope I am not wholly unreasonable in wanting to know what we have received for this $120 million. The minister has made some very general comments which I am sure are interesting but they do not answer these specific questions. I think I will understand the matter when I get the answers to these questions. If the minister agrees, I suggest that the item stand until three o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understood that the hon. member for York West had a question to ask.

Yes, my question concerns the assistance to machine tool production. I have had an opportunity to visit some of our defence plants in the last year and everywhere I went the one cry, which was I think universal, was that there is a shortage of machine tools.
Mr. Chairman, the economy of this country has now reached the stage where a growing machine tool industry must be part of that economy, and I want to ask the minister what if any assistance he has given to the establishment and the enlargement of machine tool industry in Canada. I realize that machine tools, like jet engines, are not something you can produce by turning a switch. They require a very great deal of tooling up and a very great number of experts.
In England there are some firms which have been at the production of machine tools for generations, and one firm, I understand, has now been in part at least taken over by the United Kingdom government. I refer to Herbert Alfred Limited of Birmingham, one of the major machine tool builders, and one of the very finest in the world.
I wonder whether it would be possible to have a subplant or branch of that factory or organization established in Canada. I mention this because all the production plants, almost universally, have a tremendously high opinion of the product of this firm. They just simply cannot get enough of those machine tools. As a matter of fact they cannot get enough of the United Kingdom machine tools.
I realize that everything has been done to pep up or step up production of machine tools and to get English machine tools in Canada, but apparently United Kingdom production is such that it is unlikely we are going to get machine tools from the United Kingdom in any great volume. Therefore, it would seem to me desirable, Mr. Chairman, to assist in capital expenditure for enlargement of our machine tool industry in Canada. I just wonder whether the minister has any information to give to the committee on this matter.

Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the machine tool industry of course is a private industry like any other. We have a healthy machine tool industry in this country. If any manufacturer of machine tools wishes to expand his plant to take care of government business only we will give capital assistance, and that has been done. My hon. friend will understand, however, that we do not just give capital assistance so that the machine tool man can build any kind of machine tool that he likes. If he receives capital assistance we own the machine tools, we own the plant and it can only work for the department. In other words, it must be used in business for the department. If the manufacturer wants to use it for something else, he must buy it or rent it. The machine tool industry is not the type of industry particularly adapted to capital assistance, though we have given capital assistance on two or three occasions.
The hon. member talks about the government bringing out plants from England. We depend on private industry. I think if the government brought out a machine tool manufacturer and set him up here in competition with existing industry, it might be a bit difficult. We do not do that. If a firm from the old country comes here and can do a job that we require to have done, that firm would qualify for capital assistance.
Can the minister say how much capital assistance has been given the machine tool industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not very much-it depends upon how you look at it. I do not want to be quoted by the opposition as saying a million is nothing. The capital assistance is probably around a million dollars. I take back that "not very much" and shall call it "that huge sum that weighs so heavily on the minds of the opposition."
I only mentioned this one firm because I understood it was in rather peculiar circumstances. The control of this firm is now in the hands of the United Kingdom government.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They used to have a socialist government, but we are a free enterprise government.
I entirely agree with the minister that it is not the business of government to own a plant, except where absolutely necessary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Greenwood has asked to have this item stand-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: A very unreasonable request, but perhaps we can agree to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The minister has said that some of the questions asked by the hon. member are not in order. This is a very important vote, and I should like to take the next few minutes at our disposal to examine the matter of order. It seems to me that this vote provides for $85 million for capital assistance for the construction, acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works-and so on.
Now, I understand the hon. member for Greenwood is trying to obtain some background information which would lead him to the capital assistance provided, perhaps to the company he mentioned, under this vote. If that is so, that is in order. But as the minister pointed out, when he gets into the details as to the record of the company on technical production, there may be some difficulties there in so far as relevancy is concerned. Perhaps the hon. member could enlighten the Chair on those points.

You flatter me, Mr. Chairman, but I shall at any rate express my views. When this matter was up before, we asked the minister for these contracts, which he was good enough to arrange. This was one of the contracts, and, quite apart from the contract to which we have reference, $16 million went to A. V. Roe.
The minister made quite a point of the fact that the money goes into property which remains the property of the government. It seems to me that the mere fact that this is government property which is being operated or used does not get away from the fact that A. V. Roe Canada is actually operating this property. After lunch, I hope we can find out a little of the basis upon which this is done, because it seems to me that the minister told us that no management contract had been entered into since 1949.
My point is this. Surely, when we are spending these huge amounts of money, we have not only the right but the duty to find out whether they are being successfully spent. This is a private company, but supposing it was absolutely at arm's length, which I do not think A. V. Roe is, but supposing it was, surely we would be entitled to ask something about the record of the company which is using this huge amount of government property. Actually, you cannot get any record of the A. V. Roe Company through any of the commercial agencies, because it is a privately-owned company. When you look it up, you find nothing. The only way we can find out about the efficiency of A. V. Roe, which I submit is quite relevant, is to ask something about the record of this plant which is using this very equipment running to the tune of $127 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, no, the equipment did not cost $127 million. That is it, you see; we release a few wild figures and then spread them on Hansard quite out of context in a way that may be quoted in the papers.
If the minister will allow me, I checked the figures. I read them to him and asked if they were correct. The general figure we had was in the neighbourhood of $120 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: For what?

I have the figures which the minister gave us. First of all, there was $37 million which was to be put up for the engine plant; secondly, $12 million which he called pre-production figures; thirdly, what he called a production figure of $73 million. Those are the figures that the minister gave me. I do not like to use inaccurate figures, and I checked the addition. If the minister wants to go back and change those figures-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You referred to the facilities costing $116 million, and the facilities did not cost $116 million.
Will the minister correct it, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The facilities cost $37 million, which we have approved, and of which $24 million has been paid. That is all the facilities cost. The rest will be for work and materials which will be translated into finished planes.
I say that one way or another $120 million of public moneys have gone into this operation, plants and facilities, which enable it to carry on. Is that satisfactory?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If you would say, facilities, materials and work in progress, I would be satisfied.

All right, facilities, materials and work in progress. I am as anxious to be accurate as the minister is. If I may go back, then, and complete my argument, here is $120 million of public money which is to some extent ventured in this matter. We cannot get any reports on A. V. Roe Canada, which is a privately-owned company. I submit with great earnestness, the only way we can find out about the efficiency with which this money is being spent is to get the facts as to the records. I was asking when we gave the first contract, and I propose to follow that up by asking other questions concerning what has happened since and what the situation is at the moment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It is one o'clock.
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I may add a last comment. I do not wish the hon. member to infer that I was attempting to interfere in any way with his duty to scrutinize the transaction or examine the record of whatever firm has been dealing with the government. My duty is to see that the hon. member's duty is performed at the right moment. That is my duty, and that is the only one I am performing at the moment. What puzzles me is how the hon. member is investigating the expenditure of $120 million on an $85 million vote. There must be a certain amount of that vote which is capital assistance provided to the A. V. Roe Company. I do not know how much that is, but if for instance it were $20 million, to be strictly relevant to this item the only thing that should be examined is the $20 million of capital assistance provided to the A. V. Roe. I wanted to inform the hon. member of that.
If, as background information for the examination of this $20 million of capital assistance provided by this vote, the hon. member wants to ask the minister certain questions, which he did ask, I believe that is in order, but always coming back finally to the discussion of the $20 million provided as capital assistance under this vote.
There is this matter of production. There may be a place somewhere along the line where questions can be asked about production; that is, the time at which the order was placed and other questions pertaining to the production process. There must be a place where such questions can be asked. The Minister of Defence Production has said that they should not be asked on this vote. Well, let us find out which other vote. I am sure the hon. member will be able to wait until such an occasion arises to ask his question as to production.

May I just reiterate what I said a moment ago very briefly? Surely the whole purpose of defence production, as I understand it, is to serve national defence in getting this very kind of thing done.
As to your comment, Mr. Chairman, how we can investigate $120 million in a vote of $85 million, I think you gave the answer perfectly. The money which is going in now is going into the same pot into which other large amounts have gone. I submit finally: We have no other test of the efficiency of the spending than to find out what is produced. There are people who say we have spent this money and got nothing at all. I do not say that. They say we have got nothing in the way of actual aircraft in action. I am not saying that. But I do want to find out, and I hope the minister will not maintain

Supply-Defence Production a contrary position, because I think he will acknowledge that these are fair questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The next logical question is, how many planes have you produced? And the next logical question is, how many engines have you produced? My hon. friend knows better than I do-he has been told repeatedly in committee-that there are security regulations covering these matters, and the answer cannot be given. He may dwell on it from three to six-and I am sure he will-but at six o'clock he will not have the information on how many planes have been produced and how many engines have been produced. Without these figures he cannot tell whether money invested there was invested wisely or otherwise. I mean the $116 million that he is talking about. He understands that I cannot give that information. Security regulations are decided by the army, and we have our instructions not to give numbers of products. He understands that. We will give him dates of contracts, but again I say that, where the government is contracting with itself, dates of contracts are less meaningful than they are if you are contracting with an outside firm.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Greenwood was questioning me about production at the A. V. Roe plant. I would call his attention to page 2743 of Hansard for May 30, 1952, in which I gave an analysis of the work being carried out at the A. Y. Roe plant, in some detail. I have no doubt he has read that recently. I believe that in that statement is contained much of the information he desires to ask me to give at this time.
Then, as to contracts: I have a list of the contracts between the government and A. V. Roe which I shall be glad to place on Hansard.
First is a formal agreement made May 2, 1946, executed on April 24, 1947. This is file 18-26-28, covering design and development of gas turbine engines. It includes a provision for jigs and tools. Avro is to be paid its costs of the work plus a fee of 5 per cent, but Avro is only to get 3 per cent of its progress payments. This is amended by a formal agreement dated April 13, 1948, to provide for such capital equipment as the minister may approve.
This agreement provides that Avro will obtain an undertaking from the Hawker-Siddeley Aircraft Company Limited, that it and its subsidiary and allied companies will


make available to Avro all technical information and processes which are available to any such companies in connection with the development of gas turbine engines.
This agreement also provides that the crown will make available to Avro all technical data, et cetera, relating to the design and development of gas turbine engines which are available to the crown from Turbo Research Limited. This is a former crown company, since wound up. Such data are to be used by Avro only for the purposes of this agreement.
Then, secondly, is a formal agreement made November 3, 1945, and executed on October 31, 1946. This is file 18-38-4540, covering design of jet type fighter airframes, prototypes, and spare parts necessary for the maintenance thereof during test operations. It includes a provision for jigs and tools. Avro is to be paid its costs of the work plus a fee of 5 per cent, but Avro is only to get 3 per cent of its progress payments. This is amended by three formal agreements dated January 30, 1948, November 3, 1948, and March 29, 1949, the provisions of which are covered earlier in this note.
The third is a formal agreement made May 17, 1949. This is file 18-38-87, covering the manufacture of ten only CF-100 jet fighter aircraft, known as pre-production aircraft, fitted with Orenda gas turbines, 30 spare Orendas and spares, publications, ground handling equipment, et cetera. It covers the cost of jigs and tools as approved by the minister. Avro is to be paid its costs plus a fee of 5 per cent, but is only to get 3 per cent on its progress payments.
Each of the ten aircraft was to be designed as a particular version, such as (a) dual control trainer, (b) tactical ground attack version, (c) P.R. version, special aircraft for airframe tests, et cetera.
By letter of authorization dated October 23, 1951, the ceiling of expenditure was set at $32,295,802.70 including acquisition of certain radar equipment and 2 Rolls-Royce Avon R A 2 type engines.
The fourth is a formal capital assistance agreement made December 9,	1946, file
51-R-37, covering $650,000 for equipment and office furniture for Malton and Nobel plants for use in production of gas turbine engines. Avro is to be paid its costs, but no fee.
The fifth is a formal capital assistance agreement made May 9, 1949. This is file 18-38-69, to provide machine tools and equipment and other facilities of a capital nature for the Malton and Nobel plants, for use in the production of CF-100 aircraft fitted with Orenda engines. All items of machine tools and equipment are to be approved by

the minister before acquisition, and Avro is to be paid its costs of acquisition, including engineering, planning and development costs in respect of the additional equipment, and the costs of installation and re-arrangement of the existing plant and facilities incidental to installation. No fee is to be paid to Avro.
By formal amendment No. 1, dated January 5,	1950, Avro can receive accountable
advances to cover estimated expenditures one month in advance.
By letter of authorization dated August 18,
1950,	Avro was authorized to acquire the following in addition to the machine tools and equipment covered by the formal agreement: New engine plants; re-arrangement of plant; additional machinery and equipment; extension of aircraft plant by 100,000 square feet. The formal agreement was to be amended to include these additional items.
By letter of authorization dated January 3, 1952, the deputy minister authorized a ceiling expenditure of $44,352,000.
The next is a purchase order dated May 14,
1951.	It is file B/18-38-14, serial number 2/B/112, CDEF-101, covering main production order for the CF-100 jet fighter aircraft incorporating Orenda turbine engine, and spare Orenda engines, together with spares of airframes and engines, ground handling equipment, special tools and technical publications. Then there was a purchase order dated March 19, 1952, covering metal shipping containers for Orenda engines, at a price to be negotiated.
Purchase order under file B/18-38-139 covers the overhaul and modification of approximately fourteen Lancaster aircraft on a cost plus basis.
Miscellaneous purchase orders covering the purchase of Lancaster and other spare parts on fixed catalogue prices.
Those are all the contracts entered into to date.
I take it that these contracts and figures to which the minister has referred would approximate the over-all figure that was given this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.
Reference was made to the CF-100 for training purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No. I do not like to get the record muddled up; the pre-production aircraft were not all for training purposes. There was one typical training aircraft and one typical rocket firing aircraft; in short, each one is typical of a modification of the
Supply-Defence Production aircraft that is intended to be put into production. There were ten aircraft of different types, in connection with each of which there is to be a pre-production model for development purposes.

I accept the minister's correction, but unless I misheard him he did use the word "trainer". Perhaps I took it up wrongly. Do I understand that the minister feels that the question I asked before recess as to the actual date of the order for the service plane is a matter of security?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, I gave that; it is May 14,
1951.	That was item 6 on the contracts I gave.

If there is no objection I should like the minister to tell us how many are on order, how many have been actually produced and whether they have come from an actual production line or from what was referred to in an aviation magazine as an enlarged model shop.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I cannot give that figure. My hon. friend knows from his experience in the committee on defence expenditures that the R.C.A.F. are very much against giving production figures or the total number on order. I cannot say why, but we have been informed that that is secret information and that we must observe secrecy.

Then I shall not pursue that. I take it however that there is no secrecy about what appeared in the magazine Aircraft, which is referred to as Canada's aviation news magazine. The issue of March last makes a comment on production which I think should be put on the record. Certainly it is public, and accordingly I read it. This is from the issue of March,
1952,	a statement by E. V. Rippingille, Jr., federal director of aircraft production, who says:
Avro Canada has developed not only a gas turbine but they have started to move into their new engine plant and before long they will be in production. Engines produced to date have come from an enlarged model shop. The CF-100 is still undergoing test and development but, like all aircraft, it will continue to be developed until it is fundamentally obsolete. Production is slow but is being gradually accelerated.
In the same issue there is what is termed an authoritative review of Canada's aircraft industry, from which I should like to read briefly as follows:
It is unfortunate that engineering difficulties with the CF-100 have slowed its production and delayed its getting into squadron service. It is a fact that this is an aircraft under development and as such it can't be hurried along.

Supply-Defence Production
And then later:
With few Orendas likely to he available before the beginning of 1953, it is improbable that any of the Sabres will be powered with this engine. By this time, too, enough CF-lOO's should be coming along to absorb all the initial production of Orendas.
I pass from that to ask another question which I think has been discussed in the defence expenditures committee. Is the CF-100 being fitted with modern air-to-air armaments?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Again I am told that the armament on fighter aircraft is security information. I should like to make some comment on that subject, but I cannot.

I do not know what comment I can make on that except that there ought to be a caucus of the departments. I have one or two more questions and I know the minister will be glad to be told that I am not going to take three hours, but only a few minutes. I think it is clear from the record that a large amount of money has gone into this and that the results to date so far as pace is concerned have been disappointing. From the records I have read and from other things, unless something has happened within the last few weeks, it looks as though no production in a real sense of the term has been reached.
As I pointed out this morning, it is evident that the R.C.A.F. and the manufacturers had a proper desire to build our own engine. They have been going ahead with that with disappointments. As far as I can see it is true that we have not a supply of these engines available yet and I should like to ask the minister if there was an engine that we could have had. Were the Hawker-Siddeley people manufacturing an engine which would have been useful as a stand-by and which would not have left us in the position in which we now appear to be?
