speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I suppose my hon. friend is asking whether it was wise to undertake the building of an engine?
I have said that I think that that was a proper thing to do. I am simply asking whether it might have been wise to have had a stand-by alternative.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The position is that the production of jet engines is limiting the production of complete aircraft. There are airframes all over the continent waiting for engines. The production of aircraft in Canada is limited by the supply of engines that we can make available or that are being made available to us. The Orenda will be a valuable addition to the supply of engines for allied countries.
fMr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]

We are hopeful that it will take care of the requirements of the two aircraft I have mentioned, the CF-100 and the Sabre; we believe that the timing of production will permit that to take place. We have reason to believe that the actual production of Orenda engines will be ahead of the quantity that was scheduled for production, in other words ahead of the rated capacity of the plant. I understand that expected production will take care both of the CF-100, for which it was designed, and the Sabre, which will be a greatly improved aircraft when the Orenda can be installed.

Apparently there has been in the past a lot of unwarranted optimism and I hope the minister's optimism is more warranted because he has not indulged in it in the past as other people have. The minister does not seem to have answered my question. He said that there are airframes waiting for engines and I asked whether there was any engine which we could have had. I understand the Hawker-Siddeley people have the Sapphire engine in production which might have been available if we had wanted a stand-by and it might have been useful now.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Sapphire engine has been licensed for production in the United States. I am told, however, that it will not be in actual production for several months. In other words, the Orenda engine, so far as this continent is concerned, is some months ahead of the Sapphire. There are only a few Sapphire engines being produced in the old country which are being used for United Kingdom planes, and it is impossible to obtain them for installation in Canadian aircraft.

I was aware that they were licensed for manufacture in the United States by the Curtiss-Wright people, but I did not know about Canada. He has added that. I come back to ask this question. He says that at the moment the Sapphire is not in production in England to an extent that would make any available here. Would that have been true two, three or four years ago if we had wished then to have an alternative?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There were no Sapphire engines two, three or four years ago. The development of the Sapphire engine has more or less paralleled the production of the Orenda engine. The two were started about the same time and the production of Sapphires is about as far advanced as the production of Orendas.
Then am I wrong in my information that the Sapphire is and has been for some time in real production in England?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You are quite wrong.
The minister is satisfied that is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

I want to make one or two observations. I think the whole question of security so far as the Department of Defence Production and the Department of National Defence are concerned should be examined. In my opinion more information should be available because I am sure it will not be helpful to anybody. Information is published in technical magazines, trade papers and frequently in articles by commentators in the press. I realize that an official statement is an official statement and that upon it those who are hostile to us can base their plans, but I feel that secrecy in this regard is carried to too great an extreme. There is one other point I should like to mention with respect to the A. Y. Roe company. The A. V. Roe company has a very advanced prototype of a jet liner-I think it is the only one in existence-which would give this country a tremendous advantage in the commercial production of a high speed jet short-range aircraft.
I realize that the project had to be abandoned temporarily owing to the lack of space, trained personnel and tooling. I realize that to go on with it would probably involve great expense. Far from criticizing the expense of bringing into production a new aircraft based on a prototype of this kind, particularly in conjunction with the Comet which is the long-range jet commercial liner, I think it was unfortunate to say the least that the project was abandoned. If it is at all possible I hope the A. V. Roe company will be encouraged to proceed with the construction of that aircraft.

Before the item is carried it is my desire to pay a well deserved tribute to the minister. I know of no man who could have organized Trans-Canada Air Lines as well as their operations now demonstrate. In addition, he organized the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and he provided a great impulse to Canadian business and industry to such an extent that Canada is one of the great industrial countries of the world. Therefore it is with great pleasure that I congratulate the minister on his numerous accomplishments and I hope he will stay with us long enough to make the country benefit from his wide experience and remarkable spirit of initiative.

I am glad to be able to associate myself with a good deal of what the hon. member for Temiscouata has said but that does not affect the fact that I
55704-229J
Supply-Defence Production still have one or two questions to ask. I am not quite clear on this matter and I should like to ask the minister, particularly in view of what I read from the aviation magazine, whether the CF-100 is actually coming off the production line now. Before the minister answers, may I add that I ask that question partly in view of the speech of Mr. Crawford Gordon a short while ago in which I understood there was reference to a plant for a jet engine still under construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This is what I said on May 30, 1952, as found at page 2743 of Hansard:
Deliveries of the CF-100 under the main production contract are scheduled to commence in August, 1952. For security reasons, it would be inappropriate to review our planned rate of production, but I have every reason to believe that A. V. Roe will live up to our agreed production schedule, as long as certain electronic equipment can be secured from the United States.
I might say that we are rather in advance of the production schedule. The first planes have already come off the production line. My hon. friend lives in Toronto. I suppose he visits that city occasionally and if he would spend an hour at Malton all these questions would be answered because there is a very healthy production line that can be viewed by selected personnel from the House of Commons!
I can understand the minister so much better than I could understand things if I went out to the plant myself.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
81[DOT] To provide for the liquidation of contracts, including commitments of previous years related to the acquisition of assets operated by the departments of munitions and supply and reconstruction and supply or an agency of these departments; the liquidation of the assets and liabilities of closed crown companies and crown plants; and for miscellaneous and unforeseen expenses, $150,000.
I presume this item refers to payments which will be diminishing each year. Will the minister give us an explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. We must keep a token item available for the reason that we have two or three lawsuits still before the courts. All the contracts that could be closed by negotiation have been closed and we are only providing this amount to await the result of actions before the exchequer court.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Crown companies-
82.	To provide for expenses incurred by Defepce Construction Limited in procuring the construction of defence projects on behalf of the Department of National Defence, $3,308,500.

Why did the minister's engineers select the ground they did in Cobourg for

Supply-Defence Production the ordnance building there? It is swamp land. According to a return tabled in my name, I understand that it will cost $407,250 for drainage plus $70,000 for concrete slabs to be built underneath the concrete tile. That is practically half a million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The purchasing of land and the preparation of plans for development are functions of the Department of National Defence. The Department of Defence Production only takes over when national defence is furnished with the plans and the site. From there on the Department of Defence Production is responsible for the building. My department has nothing to do with the acquisition of land.
Well, Mr. Chairman, is it not the minister's department that has the engineers .who go over the land checking the soil to see whether it is suitable for building?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If the engineers are part of the army organization they are not hired by us. If it is a firm of consulting engineers doing the job we make a contract with the firm to perform the work and after that they report to the armed services until the design is worked out. We take no responsibility for design. The functions are very sharply designed and it is the duty of the army to say what it wants-and that involves the preparation of plans-when it wants it, and then the Department of Defence Production attempts to take over from that point and give to the armed services what they want.

But is it not the minister's department which has the soil engineers who say whether the land is or is not suitable for a building of that kind? I understand that they have 80-foot piling in the building in this case but in the Royal York hotel, the tallest building in the empire, they used only 38-foot piling.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not think the length of the piling is significant. I have built grain elevators where we used 20-foot piling and in others we used 80-foot piling. I am told that the site is very suitable for the purpose but as I say it is not the function of the Department of Defence Production to acquire the land or plan the requirements of the building.

Will the minister explain the manner in which Defence Construction Limited is required to make expenditures? As I understand it the money for these defence projects is voted by the Department of National Defence. Then, the actual work is done under the Department of Defence Production through this agency or crown

company known as Defence Construction Limited. In what way is this vote of $3,308,500 to be used?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is simply to pay for the administration of the work by Defence Construction Limited. If the army wishes to build a building it sends over to the Department of Defence Production the plans for the building and a certificate of encumbrance covering the estimated cost of the building. The department then operates through this crown company, Defence Construction Limited. Defence Construction Limited proceeds to process the building, to place a contract and to inspect the work through to completion until it can be turned over to the army in a condition that is satisfactory to the army. This item is to cover the cost of engineering and other services performed by the Department of Defence Production on the building through the construction period and until it is turned over to the services.
Defence Construction Limited does not do any actual construction itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.
The work would be let out by contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

There is an increase of $1,-
100,000	odd this year. Could the minister give us some idea of why the increase was necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The increase is almost directly proportional to the amount of work the department has to handle. The more contracts there are the more inspectors and the more work generally is required. This is almost entirely payment of staff.

Where does the Department of Public Works fit into the picture? If I remember correctly before the second war defence projects were built by the Department of Public Works very much in the way in which the Department of Defence Production now builds them. Does each department carry on in the same way but with the Department of Public Works being restricted to civilian projects-or just what are the respective spheres?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is correct. In 1940 all procurement work for the services was turned over to the newly created department of munitions and supply. That included all building projects required for the services and all procurement for the services. That is the situation that has obtained since that -time. In other words, in 1940 the work was transferred from the Department of Public Works to the department of munitions and

supply. The Department of Public Works is responsible for building for other than the armed services and the Department of Defence Production is responsible for building for the armed services.
In the case of airports, since the Department of Transport has a trained staff familiar with airport work, at my request the Department of Transport has relieved the Department of Defence Production of building runways. Similarly, since Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has the necessary staff and is familiar with the building of housing, the housing work for the Department of Defence Production has, at my request, been turned over to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and is carried out by them. That is simply a matter of using the best facilities that the government has available.

The minister said a few days ago that he did not expect the Department of Defence Production to be carried on indefinitely. I presume that in due course this work of building projects for the Department of National Defence will revert to the Department of Public Works? Is that the intention?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is a matter that cannot be predicted at this time. When the work handled by the Department of Defence Production becomes so small that it does not warrant the overhead of a separate department, the work will be placed elsewhere; but I cannot predict at this time where the work will be placed.

Who carries on the day-to-day inspections on these various construction projects-the Department of Defence Production or the Department of National Defence? I would take it that it would be the Department of National Defence. They take over the projects and would have to pass on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The day-to-day inspection is carried on by the Department of Defence Production. When the work is ready to be turned over to the Department of National Defence, that department has to be satisfied with it or it will not accept the project; but up to that point, the inspection is the "responsibility of the Department of Defence Production.
I wonder if the minister has a statement of the projects that are being constructed in the province of Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, I am afraid not.

Perhaps I could get that.
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You can get that at any time from the department.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Canadian Arsenals Limited-
83.	Administration and operation, $750,000.
Will the minister explain the position of Canadian Arsenals Limited at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Canadian Arsenals Limited is a corporation formed to take over those installations of the last war which it was felt should be maintained as part of the permanent defence of Canada. A committee of the armed services and the department of munitions and supply studied the matter very carefully for a considerable period and made a report which recommended that certain plants be retained. It is the duty of Canadian Arsenals Limited to look after those plants, keep them ready for operation, and produce up to the capacity of the plants the peacetime requirements of the armed services.
The peacetime requirements?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Requirements of the armed services between wars are of course peacetime requirements. At the moment the arsenal plants are working to capacity and they are accounting for a considerable part of the production of munitions of the present' day.
Can the minister say how much work is being done in Canadian Arsenals on NATO account?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is difficult to say. The work on NATO account is an extension of the work on Canadian account. We are doing nothing for NATO that is not an extension of the work for Canada. At the moment, I presume the plants are working on Canadian production, although several of them have contracts for NATO which will follow on as soon as the Canadian requirements are met.

I know they are doing work for NATO, but I wanted to know whether the contracts are paid for through NATO. Do we pay for the equipment, deliver it to NATO and take credit for our part in the NATO establishment?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is correct.
There is no monetary transaction from NATO to Canadian Arsenals?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

These things we produce form a part of our contribution to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization?

Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is true in part, although countries in the NATO group have placed orders in Canada tor cash. For example, the United Kingdom is buying certain things in Canada and paying cash, but there is also certain equipment being furnished as a result of the Canadian contribution to NATO and that material is paid for out of Canada's appropriation for NATO. The finished material delivered to NATO forms part of Canada's contribution.
And the charge to NATO, I presume, is at cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

There is one question which goes back to the previous item which perhaps the minister would answer. He told us that in 1946 and in 1947, one of those years, there was a sale to A. V. Roe for $2 million, and it was paid in cash. Has any money from outside gone into A. V. Roe since then, except from the government of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, from cash sent out from England or credits arranged in Canada and backed by Avro of England. The Avro investment in its Canadian operation is about $16-5 million at the present time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Canadian Arsenals Limited-[DOT]
84.	Construction, improvements and new equipment, $1,650,000.

According to the details covering this item there was only $500,000 expended during the last fiscal year. The vote for this year is $1,650,000. Can the minister explain why there has been an increase of over $1 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman; the vote for last year was $1,700,000. We are stepping up the capacity of the arsenal to take care of current requirements. For instance, we have reactivated the explosives plant at DeSalaberry, to fill orders for explosives for our own services and others. We are extending the plant at St. Paul l'Ermite to take care of shell filling, which in the last war was carried on at three or four plants. In Quebec, we are extending the capacity to make shell cases. At Long Branch we are setting up a new line for small arms.
Apparently, the expenditure last year was only $500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It may be-the payments, you mean, were only $500,000?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I presume a large part of the balance is a carry-over from last year.

This is an additional vote of $25 million for capital assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
National Research Council-
295. Salaries and other expenses, $12,198,684.

This is the administration item for the national research council, and it shows an increase of a little over $1-5 million. Gan the minister explain why there is an increase? I must admit that I am biased in favour of the research council, but perhaps the minister can tell us why there is that increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is due to an extension of activities during the period of defence production. There are certain calls on the facilities of the research council that are abnormal

and call for more staff and greater activity. The activities of the national research council are expanding from year to year, but the expansion is greater than usual this year.
What progress is being made with the branches of the research council which are being established in different parts of the country outside Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The prairie laboratory has been making great progress with research on agricultural wastes, attempting to find a practical use for them. It has a very active program which I believe is welcome so far as the prairie provinces are concerned.
The maritime laboratory was opened only on Monday of last week, but we expect a very active program there, concentrating on the problems of the maritime provinces.
Can the minister give us any details of the problems which will be considered there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: A specialist on seaweed is, I believe, one of the staff. Seaweed can be developed into edible products that are considered quite valuable. I have a statement here which does not mean very much to me. I will send it over to my friend. It refers to problems of biology and chemistry and biochemistry.
Is there any thought of establishing branches in any other parts of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, the national research council has a working arrangement, for example, with a new chemistry building that I was privileged to open in British Columbia, part of the university of British Columbia, and also has arrangements with a number of universities. I know of no plans to build branch laboratories in other parts of Canada. I think the proposal is to work with existing laboratories.

What is the situation with regard to bringing students and graduates to Ottawa for work under the research council? At the time that we had a special committee of the house on the national research council we were given details of that program, and it seemed to be an extremely worth-while one. Has it been continued? What is the situation at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There are about 60 students working in the national research council at the present time. Many of them are from other countries. They are working under special students' arrangements, and it seems to be working very well. Most empire countries are represented. I think other countries
Supply-Defence Production are represented as well. We consider it a very valuable part of the work of the research council.
Is the council doing anything in connection with the Colombo plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, I think not. I am sure the council would be glad to undertake problems related to the Colombo plan, if the problems were placed in its hands; but to date the Colombo plan has involved more practical development work. For instance, fisheries experts from Vancouver have been in Ceylon; cement experts from eastern Canada have been in India. The work of the Colombo plan to date is not work that is adapted to the national research council.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Atomic energy control board-[DOT]
297. Administration expenses of the atomic energy control board, $59,302.
Will the minister say how the production of uranium ore is coming along in Canada? Is there anything he may usefully say about the mining of uranium ore in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The present Eldorado property at Great Bear lake is working at capacity. Unfortunately a fire at the mine last November burned down a number of the buildings. They were rebuilt during the winter months and were back in operation about the first of May. The mining did not stop, but delivery of ore was stopped owing to the fact that the crushing plant went out of action. During last winter a leeching plant was erected to work over the tailings of earlier ores. The tailings had been preserved and are now being put through the leeching plant, which means stepping up the output of uranium to a very considerable percentage.
As far as Beaverlodge development is concerned, the report of Eldorado, which I tabled yesterday, gives quite a detailed account of progress at that place. We are in process of building a mill. We believe that we have a very large deposit of low-grade uranium ore. We shall have a very sizeable production. Canada used to be the second largest producer of uranium. It has slipped down to third place, and we expect that when Beaverlodge goes into production we shall come back to second place.

I should like to express appreciation of the work that is done under this department. We had a very gifted young lady from Fort William working for the government in New York. She was taken seriously ill with cancer. She was rushed to the city of London and was give treatment. She is now up and out of bed. I commend the minister and his workers for this type of

Supply-Defence Production work and we hope that they will continue and develop; we also hope that this young girl will be completely cured.

In the report of the Eldorado company, which we received the other day, I noticed that it is a paying proposition at the present time. It is really a good company. When we see it in the condition in which it is I often wonder whether that company will ever reimburse the shareholders who paid enormous prices for their stock and received only a small pittance for it. From time to time these complaints come in. No doubt they have come in to the minister, because when a backbencher like myself gets them by the score, indicating that some men paid as high as $11.75 for their stock and others more than that, and received only a small pittance when the government took over the company, surely he must get complaints as well. Now, since the company has commenced to pay, surely he will reimburse these men for what they paid for the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: When the government took over the property it was not in the condition that it is in today. It had never been a paying proposition. The government offered slightly more for the shares than the market price of that day. Whether the stock was delivered or not was quite voluntary. I think practically all the stock has been turned in. I know of only one shareholder who keeps alive the complaint, and I think his holding is something less than 1,000 shares, representing about $1,200. I hardly think that complaints from the shareholders are as serious as my hon. friend would suggest. Has he had complaints from great numbers or from just one?
No; I have had complaints from a great many more than one.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not know how it would be possible at this stage to reimburse each shareholder for what he paid for his stock. I do not think that it ever sold as high as $11. It might have sold for $4 and maybe $5. To determine what people paid someone else for their shares would be a very difficult proposition.
What is the position of the shareholders? Do they receive the annual report?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There are no shareholders
other than the government.
I was just wondering.

This is the first item on atomic energy and there are one or two questions I should like to place before the minister. First of all, with regard to the sale of isotopes,

when the minister was speaking on a supplementary item of last year's estimates to be found at page 967 of Hansard for the current session he said:
There are many who feel that the dividends from the isotope field alone may well repay all the money spent for atomic energy.
But in the report of Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited, which we received a day or two ago, there is a statement about the marketing of isotopes which is not so optimistic. At page 9 the president says:
During the year, an increasing emphasis has been placed on the development of markets for other radioactive isotopes. While there is a growing demand for radioactive isotopes, it has not been possible as yet to establish this business on a profitable basis.
There was a net loss of $63,521 on the sale of radioactive isotopes during 1951. In order that the isotope development and marketing program might be carried out with greater efficiency, it became apparent that a building was required to house research, development and processing facilities, and sales and servicing staffs. The building will be located at Ottawa since this location is in reasonable proximity to the Chalk River project, the source of supply of radioactive isotopes and, at the same time, is readily accessible to the company's customers.
I would ask the minister to deal with that situation.
Then a further question has to do with the use of atomic energy for power plants of various kinds. We do not have very full information on these developments, but we read stories of the United States government making arrangements with private corporations for the development of these power plants. I would ask the minister to tell us whether Canada has some plan of that kind in contemplation. It is only a few months ago that a new crown company was set up, known as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, and we were told at that time that the main reason for the setting up of this company was the prospect for the early and useful industrial application of atomic energy. I am wondering what progress Canada has made along these lines, and whether it is the government's intention to use private industry to help in the development of these plants.
Then, finally, we read in the press that the Prime Minister of Australia is here primarily to try to make some arrangements for assistance in establishing an atomic energy plant or for the mining of uranium in Australia. Would the Minister of Defence Production make a statement in that connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
When I spoke of some persons feeling that the dividends from isotopes alone might justify all the government's expenditures in connection with atomic energy, I did not mean a return in dollars and cents. I think the sale of isotopes can be put on a

profitable basis, and at the present time there is a great deal of development work going on designed to interest Canadian industry in the use of isotopes.
What I meant was that the results to humanity, if we may put it that way, or to the over-all economy, might justify all the expenditure. For example, how can one place a value on the life of the woman to whom the hon. member for Fort William referred a short time ago. We have two cobalt-60 bombs in operation. I am told they are bringing about remarkable recoveries in cancer cases. We hope that during this year we will have six more in operation. I might say that the demand for the bomb is far beyond any likelihood of being met. At the present time Canada is the only country capable of producing cobalt-60. That will be a fine contribution to humanity.
Then there are plant studies taking place. These are efforts to trace the effect of the various components in the soil on plant growth. These studies might very easily contribute a result that would be a national benefit. It was these intangible values, intangible so far as dollars and cents are concerned, to which I was referring when I said that isotopes might justify all expenditures to date.
Then, answering the hon. member's second question as to the progress being made in the application of atomic energy for the production of power, we are approaching the stage where practical results can be obtained. For example, we all know that an atomic power plant is being put in a submarine.
In the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, in the United States; at New London, Connecticut. We know that in the United States progress is being made in connection with pilot plants for producing useful energy from atomic energy. At Chalk River we are in process of constructing a larger pile which will permit wider development in the practical application of atomic power; and great progress is being made in working out the details of a process for transforming atomic energy into useful energy. At the moment we have not been active in building an actual and practical plant to convert one to the other; but we are well on the way toward that objective. I said before it is our belief that by 1960 atomic energy would be in practical use on a large scale for producing power from atomic sources.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes.
Supply-Defence Production
The minister did not answer my question concerning the use of industry in this development.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: On the directorate of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited we have placed practical men from industry. There are four or five men from the large electrical power companies, and one or two others from industry generally. We hope that as a result of their contact with atomic energy we will get a directive as to how best to proceed with the practical development of atomic power.
There is no private industry helping at the moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, not at the moment.
Now, would the minister answer my question with regard to Australia.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sorry to say that I have not yet met the Prime Minister of Australia, though I hope to do so this evening. But so far as I can learn he has nothing to ask of Canada with regard to the mining or refining of uranium ore. I may be wrong in that; but that is my present information.

The minister suggested that by 1960 atomic energy would be available in substantial quantities for the production of electrical power. He also said that some of the directors of the company are associated with the electrical industry, and that he is hoping to get some directive from them.
I presume the minister has in mind the fact that the development of this power would present particular opportunities to the eastern part of Canada. In British Columbia there is an extensive development of hydroelectric energy in the mountains. Then there is the vast oil industry of the prairies. I presume the Minister of Transport would certainly say there will be additional hydroelectric energy from the St. Lawrence development.
This leaves a wonderful opportunity for hydroelectric development in the ' maritime provinces. I am not sure how many of the directors are associated with electrical energy development in the maritimes. I realize there may be some question raised by interests there as to what development should take place. But I do urge upon the minister the desirability and, indeed, the necessity for increasing power development in that area, if we are to have the industrial development we are seeking. Such development we all realize is dependent to a substantial extent upon additional power facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am well aware that areas such as the maritime provinces, that have not a plentiful supply of hydroelectric power, will benefit particularly from the development of atomic power. With that thought in mind I

Supply-Defence Production have put on the board a brilliant Nova Scotian, who was a student of mine at Dal-housie, in the person of Geoffrey Gaherty, one of the great engineers in this country. I am sure he will keep the needs of the maritime provinces in mind.
