speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxion (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope it would
meet the convenience of hon. members of this committee if there were an understanding along similar lines to that which we have had over the last four or five years regarding the method of proceeding with the discussion of these estimates. On previous occasions it has been understood, agreed, and generally followed that we should begin with a general discussion on this item and then when that is concluded proceed to deal with the navy, army and air force in that order, taking up the main subheadings, and then follow that with defence research and any other items. I take it that is the general view of the committee as to the most orderly way in which we can proceed.

It is not my intention to make a speech covering the whole ground of defence. We have already had three days' discussion on a motion to go into supply. That discussion took place on April 3, 4 and 8. In addition, there have been other debates dealing with defence matters which occurred on May 2, 12, 13, 19 and 20. There was an extended and detailed consideration of defence matters in the committee on defence expenditures which made its report to the house on June 10. Here I should like to express my own appreciation to the members of that committee for the very hard work they did on this very important subject. There was also a white paper tabled last Friday which covers the ground in a general way and also deals with defence expenditure and the appropriations under various heads.
It occurred to me that the most useful thing I might do at this time would be to touch on the highlights of the events of the last two years and then discuss with hon. members some of the problems with which we find it most difficult to deal in the years that lie ahead. Before doing that, however, I think you would expect me to say a few words about the general international situation, the climate which determines the temperature of the cold war. You will agree that lately there has been some evidence of a general feeling that the tension has relaxed. The impression has apparently been created somehow that for some reason the international situation has improved. Subject to one important exception, which I will mention later, I can see no fact, no event, no development which would justify this more optimistic outlook.
As to what are the reasons for the change in public sentiment, one guess is as good as another. One view might be that it is due to the rash of elections here and elsewhere. People do not like to be taxed for anything, and that includes defence. In the atmosphere of an election, whether it be in the United States, Canada or elsewhere, the natural tendency is for it to be said that taxes are too high; and this leads by a perfectly natural process to the feeling that one of the principal causes of high taxes, namely defence expenditures, is not as necessary as we thought a few months ago.
What is the position? No one I know in a position of authority or responsibility believes that war is likely in the near future; but no one knows that there will not be war and nothing has occurred to make the danger of war less than it was two years ago except perhaps the very fact that we have been successful in avoiding war over a difficult

period. Whether it be due to what our allies and ourselves have done in building up our strength to prevent aggression under the North Atlantic treaty, or whether it has been due to what our allies and ourselves have done to stop aggression under the United Nations effort in Korea; whether it be due to the industrial or economic strength-yes, the strength of the ideals of the freedom loving nations-the fact is that since the North Atlantic treaty was signed three years ago we have had three years of freedom from war.
Our experience before 1949 led us to enter into the North Atlantic treaty in order to build strong foundations for freedom and peace. That decision was entered into, that decision has been acted upon, the treaty was made, the build-up is occurring and we have succeeded in achieving that avoidance of war which was our original goal. There is no ground for discouragement; there is no cause for complacency; there is no reason for retreat. We are doing what we set out to do, and so far we are succeeding in our purpose.
Having set our hand to the plow, having tooled up the factories, recruited and trained troops, we must continue the difficult task of maintaining our effort. The necessity for taking this attitude, the need for continuing effort, and the difficulty we can expect to meet in obtaining continued support for what is needed have been pointed out by me on numerous occasions over the last three or four years. So I make two points at the outset. First, there is no cause for retreat, discouragement or complacency. Second, we must face the necessity of continuing this effort until some other foundation for security is found.
Now, against the background of these general remarks and the other discussions that have taken place, I would like to review in the briefest form some of the things we have been doing about defence since Korea -that is, just two years ago. Two years ago today, on June 24, 1950, we had a defence budget of $425 million. We planned to build up to a strength of possibly 50,000 officers and men of the three services and we had practically stopped recruiting because we were within sight of that goal. That was two years ago today; but two years ago tomorrow, on June 25, 1950, the communists ruthlessly made their unprovoked act of aggression on South Korea with the result that, under the leadership of the United States, the United Nations intervened to stop that aggression. Then and only then the United Nations and the North Atlantic treaty
Supply-National Defence nations realized that they must speed up the further expansion of their defence activities.
Following the October meetings of the North Atlantic treaty defence ministers at which defence requirements and plans were agreed to for the first time, we arrived at a three-year program, just like all the other nations; and that was announced to this house on February 5, 1951, and has since been acted upon.
I should add, however, that no program is static, that already we are extending our defence programming to the end of 1955 and into 1956. We are now seeing the results of the speed-up of this expanded program as it was affected by the events which occurred two years ago tomorrow. We are now beginning to see the tangible results in forms which can be seen by the Canadian people. In those two years, in the navy we have had continuously on duty in Far Eastern waters three destroyers which have given a good account of themselves. Orders have been placed for 54 new vessels. Seven have been launched and 19 more will be launched this year. We are meeting our commitments under the North Atlantic treaty for the current year, having 24 ships employed in the North Atlantic regional group in addition to the ships we have for the defence of our coastal waters and harbours.
Over forty members of this parliament saw the ceremonies that took place at Sorel just ten days ago which marked further stages in our defence program with equipment for the navy and army. There was the sponsoring of two new vessels, H.M.C.S. Labrador, a new Arctic patrol vessel, and the minesweeper Chignecto. More striking was the delivery of the first 3-inch 50 calibre navy gun. Hon. members will be struck as those who went to Sorel were struck with the size of the plant and the complexity of the operation it had to do. Just three figures point this out. Each gun-each of these 3-inch 50 calibre guns-has 28,000 parts. It took 20,000 drawings and 30,000 different machine operations to bring them to that unusual state of acceptability remarked upon by the U.S. naval ordnance and referred to by the admiral representing the U.S. navy on that occasion as well as by the Minister of Defence Production on a previous occasion in this house.
Naval training is being pushed ahead for officers, tradesmen and ratings. A new school was opened at H.M.C.S. Montcalm at Quebec city for French replacements and it is now going ahead with its full planned quota.
As regards the army, since Korea we have raised the 25th brigade for service there. Its

Supply-National Defence splendid work and reputation speak for it better than any words of mine could, do. The 27th brigade was similarly raised for service in Europe and has just completed extensive manoeuvres. Meanwhile, in addition to raising men for these forces, we have raised men to provide for rotation and maintenance of the forces we have for the defence of Canada.
We have continued the airlift to Korea without fatal or serious accident and with indeed that remarkable record of performance which has characterized all the transport operations of the R.C.A.F. We now have three Sabre squadrons in England waiting to take their place in Europe. This represents a significant strengthening of the air defence of that part of the North Atlantic area. Other squadrons will be built up as aircraft and aircrew become available and as airfields are ready. The chances are that the limiting factor on the arrival and participation of our squadrons under the North Atlantic treaty will not be either aircraft or aircrew but airfields. All these had be timed in together, but it all has moved forward so that we hope to keep up, and I hope we are going to keep up, the rather difficult target I set of having a squadron brought into existence about every two months. The R.C.A.F. operates 31 training establishments, and I think 32 flying fields.
Territorial defence is moving along. We shall be bringing into operation in successive months some of the large permanent radar stations which will take the place of the temporary stations on which we have had to rely up to date. In addition to this contribution of practical assistance to the United Nations and North Atlantic organizations, we have in two years given or offered equipment and ammunition totalling $273 million, and provided training facilities at a cost of $48 million.
During the two years since Korea we have taken into the armed forces, that is the regular forces, a total of 70,000 officers and men. I do not believe the Canadian people have begun to realize just how big this whole operation has been, and how big it has become during this period. Consider it; 70,000 officers and men taken into the armed forces, and of course a considerable number have been lost through casualties and other wastage.
Having said something about the progress, I should like to say something about the problems that arise in connection with a program of this size and scope. The last figure I gave, of 70,000 men and women taken into the armed forces in the two years
since Korea, has been in part made necessary by the principle of rotation. So far as I know this is the first time in Canadian history that we have had a considerable force abroad in peacetime, and have had to face the necessity of maintaining them at the same time. I announced that if the military situation permitted we would rotate men after they had served a year in the Far East. The announcement was in the following terms:
As long as the military situation permits, men will be eligible for return to Canada who have approximately twelve months' service in the theatre, but no man should be required to serve more than one winter in Korea.
I am glad to say it has proved possible to carry this out as planned. Brigade headquarters opened at Pusan in Korea on May 5, 1951. The last unit of the original brigade arrived back in Canada June 5, 1952, and rotation will be completed when approximately 1,100 personnel who are to sail from Japan towards the end of June arrive in Canada on July 10. The men who have returned to Canada and stay in the armed forces, remain in the second battalions of the R.C.R., the Princess Patricia's and the Royal 22nd. Armoured corps men have been posted to the Lord Strathcona's and the R.C.D.'s. In Korea their places were taken by the first battalions of the infantry regiments and by the first regiment of the R.C.H.A.
We have formed in Canada another brigade, now largely at Wainwright training, replacing those now in Korea. Where before Korea we had in existence one battalion of each of the R.C.R.'s, Princess Patricia's, and Royal 22nd, a regiment of armour and a regiment of artillery, R.C.D.'s and Lord Strathconas, making a total of only six major units, today we have twenty-two major units either in Canada or abroad. This represents a considerable problem in rotating forces and in providing accommodation, about which I shall have something to say.
At the same time the 27th brigade is in Europe. It is a highly trained fighting unit in tip-top shape. The arrangement there is that married men will be returned to Canada after one year abroad and single men after two years. This will mean that rotation will be, in the first instance, on an individual or sub-unit basis. The men to do this are now training in Canada, mostly at Wainwright. The first of these men to return will be coming back around November or December. It does not seem very long since I saw them on their arrival at Rotterdam in November of last year.
Experience I think has shown that the period of a year for Europe is hardly economic, even when the men arrive trained up to unit standards. Also having different

periods of rotation for married and single men complicates the operation. What we propose to work toward, and what we hope we will be able to work toward, is to have the period of service established at eighteen months for everyone, working into replacement by units so that men stay with their friends and keep the unit spirit. With the men at present abroad we shall adhere to the intention expressed-it was not an undertaking-when they went abroad.
One very useful result of rotation is that the Canadian armed forces will, to an extent never before possible, be increasingly composed of men who will have had post-war experience and training, either under combat conditions in Korea or under conditions which obtain in Germany where they are able to engage in large scale manoeuvres as a brigade or part even of larger formations. If war does occur, the Canadian forces will have a hard core of officers and men who will not be seeing active service outside Canada for the first time.
Then, in addition, we shall have available in Canada a considerable number of officers and men who, having seen service in Korea or Germany or in Canada, have since left the ranks for one reason or another. At the present time there are some 27,000 officers and men who have retired from the armed forces since the end of the second world war, and who to a considerable extent constitute a readily available reserve, adding to the reserve we always have in the reserve forces.
In order to carry out a policy of rotation, it is necessary to have a formation in Canada, or its equivalent, duplicating each formation abroad. It is necessary to have men in readiness, in a condition of training so that they can take their places in replacing their comrades either in action in Korea or in training in Germany. The intention is that the operation be carried on without a break. The performance of those returning will be equalled by the performance of those replacing them; so far that has proved possible. In the case of the army, as I said this means that for every formation abroad there must be a corresponding formation at home. In the case of the navy we have employed five ships to keep three in the field. In the case of the air force we have gradually worked through several hundred more officers and men, both aircrew and ground crew, than have been employed at any time on the air lanes to Japan. Meanwhile of course we have to maintain in Canada the mobile striking force. On previous occasions I have given reasons why this formation cannot be used for purposes of rotation; but this must not be
Supply-National Defence regarded as in any sense a static formation. The men who returned from Korea and stayed on in the armed forces are largely now in the mobile striking force, and many of them are undergoing airborne and arctic training. All of them will have that in time. Altogether we now have in the armed forces more than 3,500 officers and men who have had airborne training, and you see them in all types of formations.
As I have said, where we had two years ago six major formations, today we have twenty-two; and this points up the problem of providing accommodation for the armed forces.
We will have to relocate a number of major units at various places across Canada, and this will enable us to give a much more satisfactory geographic distribution of major units than has ever been possible before. The great majority of these units will be established at existing camps not far from urban centres or at places to be built close to urban centres. It is not our intention to relocate the permanent headquarters of these major formations at isolated centres. Camps like Wainwright* and Shilo, which are fairly isolated, will be used as training schools, but major units will not be located at those places. While they are fine training areas, Borden and Meaford no longer provide quite the range and variety of ground needed for the employment of artillery and tanks in all respects, and it would be costly, both in money and in the employment of useful agricultural land, to enlarge either of those areas very much. Accordingly we will be moving the armour school to Shilo, where the artillery school is already established and there, with the addition of some land at relatively little cost, we will have an area sufficiently large to enable us to train both armour and artillery on a considerable scale.
The school staffs at Shilo and the build-up of other formations at Borden will mean that all available accommodation will be used at both places, and indeed we will have to continue to construct more accommodation at Borden.
What I have said makes it evident that we will need assistance and widespread support to continue to secure the men we want. It is terribly important to make the young men of our country feel that they are needed in the armed forces; to make the members of the armed forces feel that they are members of the community, that they belong to the community, that they matter to the community, and that they are supported by the community. For every story of disorder or crime on the part of the armed forces that may be played up in the press, there are

Supply-National Defence two hundred records of useful service that, unfortunately but naturally, are never noticed. Because of this we in national defence, yes, we in parliament, must do everything we can to ensure that the services deserve a good name and that they have a good name.
Closely associated with obtaining the men and women we want is their training in leadership. Increasing the size of the armed forces from 47,000 to 97,000 in the two years has meant a brand new problem in officer production. During that time we were able to add 6,500 officers to the regular forces. In the white paper reference is made to my announcement of February 5, 1951, that the planned peak of the regular forces was 115,000. The figure now works out, according to our plans, to something in the neighbourhood of
120.000	from 1954 on. This has created a continuing need greater than that which could be filled through the existing officer training establishments. Accordingly we worked out, and on June 12 I announced, three important changes or rather developments in the arrangements for training officers. These were, first, a two-year course at the service colleges or universities for officers not requiring technical qualifications; second, assistance to candidates who engage to serve for at least three years after they are commissioned, and third, the establishment of a new Canadian service college cadet school at St. Johns in the province of Quebec.
Through these means we should be able to get the number of officers required after the forces have reached their planned strength. In the meantime we estimate that we have about 50,000 veteran officers still fit to serve who could be available to meet, and so enable us to meet, an emergency without any difficulty if it occurred in the near future, pending the increase in the training facilities that I have referred to.
Our reserve forces continue to be of the utmost importance, and they receive all possible assistance and support. But it is no part of the role of the reserve forces to furnish front-line strength ready at any moment to fight a trained enemy abroad. Their job, and I refer to the army particularly, remains what it was in the first and second world wars in which they did so well. The strength of the reserve forces of the tnree services since Korea has increased from
50.000	to 57,000. The aspect of their role, to which I have just referred, is brought out by the fact that another 7,600 members of the reserve forces have joined the active forces during this period of two years.
I have mentioned the all-important question of manpower and leadership. We want
fMr. Claxton. i
men of the type we have, and they need the best kind of equipment. Here the problem of defence planning becomes most difficult during a period of transition, and this is a period of transition. If there were a war today the weapons used would be largely those of the second world war. The only substantial improvements would be in long-range heavy bombers, the effectiveness of radar, the better performance of anti-tank weapons and, perhaps most important, the great improvement in the performance of jet fighters.
It is always a difficult question in a period of rearmament to know when to cease development and commence production. The work of development must be carried on mainly by our larger partners, and for us the question generally is when to purchase or put into production in Canada a model of equipment developed elsewhere. If this is too soon, the weapon may be obsolescent when it is most needed. If it is left too late, we may lack the weapons we need.
It is of course out of the question for a country like Canada to keep re-equipping with each succeeding development. We cannot afford to introduce developments which represent only marginal improvements. In this field one can never be sure that one's judgment is right except in relation to the past and reasonably near future, and errors of judgment are possible. So far, however, we seem to have steered the right course. For example, had we gone into the production of aircraft like the Vampire Mark III or Mark V and certain types of other weapons, as was sometimes suggested, we would now have the armed forces equipped with weapons that were already becoming obsolete. As it is we are producing the latest types of equipment we know of, well up in line with the United States and the United Kingdom.
Mention of our two largest partners brings me to the question of standardization. The ABC committees, as they are called, consist of representatives of the United States, Great Britain and Canada, and they are continuing to work on standardization within the framework of NATO. One branch for which we are responsible has to do with all matters relating to mapping. This work is complete, and has been accepted. Very considerable progress has been made in the standardization of battle procedures. This has been agreed to for the navy, and agreed to in part for the army and the air force. There has also been an acceptance of standard practices regarding communications.

As regards weapons, steady but unspectacular progress is being made. As new weapons are on the secret list until brought into operational use, it is not possible to report in detail. But I can tell hon. members that the other countries concerned have shown very considerable interest in the developments we have been making in regard to light wireless sets, flame throwers, anti-tank weapons and vehicles for use in winter under arctic conditions, as well as in a number of other lines.
While experience in Korea has shown that it is possible without too great difficulty to supply troops using different types of weapons and ammunition, there can be no doubt that the advantages of all using the same type would be very considerable. The difficulties in this respect of the aggressors in Korea make this quite clear.
Here I may point out that the United States, the United Kingdom and ourselves are using 3-5-inch army rocket-launchers, 3-inch 50 calibre naval guns, 75 mm. recoilless rifles and various types of aircraft, machine guns, rockets, torpedoes and anti-submarine bombs. On a large range of weapons we have reached agreement on the desirable military charac-teristcs, and design and development are being pressed on by the various teams.
In the case of the rifle and small arms generally, I have previously reported on the position taken by Canada. When it was announced in April, 1951, that the United Kingdom would proceed with the -280, our intervention resulted in a meeting at Washington in August and in further consideration of the problem by a committee of high ranking officers under North Atlantic treaty arrangements.
The present position is that the Americans, because of their large stocks, are prepared to continue to use the M2 semi-automatic Garand with the -30 rimless cartridge for a considerable period ahead. They are continuing to work on design and development of a new round and rifle having the agreed military characteristics. The British are working towards the same agreed characteristics, largely with the -280.
We hope that it might be possible to produce a round which would combine the characteristics of the British bullet and the United States cartridge, and accordingly we are doing research and development work on this with the support of both the British and United States partners. This work is being undertaken by a team representing Canadian Arsenals Limited, the defence research council and the Canadian army. We will keep in close touch with corresponding teams working
Supply-National Defence in Great Britain and the United States. From discussions I have bad in Washington with the secretary of the army, Hon. Frank Pace, and with Lord Alexander, secretary of defence in the United Kingdom, during the last week, it is evident that there will be a full interchange of information and a genuine effort to arrive at a common goal. As it is, the British and American weapons that have been designed and are in process of further development are very much closer to each other than they were a year ago.
Like the British, we are tooled up to make the -303 rifle and round and have a sufficient number of these to enable us to meet any current requirements and, pending further production, to equip our forces. Should this become necessary in another world war we could go into production at a high rate on the existing -303 rifle and round in a short time.
Until the end product of this development effort by the countries concerned becomes more evident, it would obviously be unwise for us today to go into the production of more than the minimum needed to fill immediate needs. Everyone at some time is going to adopt a new rifle and round. When that [DOT]time may be, it is impossible to say.
As regards field guns, we are making the 155 millimetre American-type gun for ourselves, for the United States, and for mutual aid to North Atlantic nations. This gun, like the ships to which I referred and the 3-inch 50 calibre gun, is being produced at Sorel, and quantity production will begin before many months are passed. At Sorel production is also being undertaken on the 120 millimetre gun for the United States army.
Anti-tank weapons and mortars are largely accepted as standard and both weapons and ammunition are being produced in Canada today.
Another problem presented by our type of force particularly is the standard of living we are going to provide for our armed forces. We have set as the right standard the standard of living which men of similar education and aptitude would obtain in corresponding civilian occupations with good employers. The committee on defence expenditure went into this and I am not going into it in any detail now. Moreover, there are some interesting figures in the white paper.
There are one or two points, however, to which I should further refer, particularly on construction. I mention this because people are surprised at the amount of construction we are finding it necessary to undertake. This year we are seeking a total of $563 million for construction, part of it to be met out

Supply-National Defence of cash appropriations for this year, and part out of commitments for future years. Of this we expect to spend $244 million in the current year, as compared to $92 million in 1940-41 or $152 million for the wartime peak year of 1943-44, and $173 million for last year.
The reason for part of this construction is doubling the size of the regular forces in the two years since Korea. An increase from
47,000	to 97,000 means that we have to find accommodation somewhere for the single men and the married men and their families equivalent to a city having a total population of 50,000. That is a lot of construction.
Wherever possible this is found through the renovation of wartime huts; but there is a limit, physical as well as financial, to what can properly be done along these lines. These huts were only expected to have a life of four or five years and for the most part were built in the cheapest and quickest way that could be found. A two-storey air force H hut cost $59,500 in 1941 and accommodated 304 men on a double-bunk basis. It now accommodates 168 men on a single bed basis after renovation. Today it costs about $100,000 to renovate such a hut; and that has been done with all the huts in locations where they can be used. That gives them an extra life of about 30 years.
To build a new R.C.A.F. barrack block for 250 men costs a total of $592,590. That allows about eighty square feet of space per man, which is about what is laid down by health authorities. This provides for four men in a room 16 by 20 feet, and it is contemplated that in an emergency we would have double decker beds and so double this accommodation.
In addition officers and men must have mess halls. and kitchens. The standard mess hall seats 500 men and has kitchen equipment that can deal with 1,000. The type of building, the amount of space, the quality of furniture and the kitchen equipment are about what you will find in an average cafeteria. This building is done for us by Defence Construction Limited, as agent for the Department of Defence Production.
Married quarters are built according to designs worked out by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and provide similar standards of accommodation to those used by C.M.H.C. in housing projects and veterans' plans across the country. We collect for rent for these houses an amount which varies in proportion to the subsistence allowance for the married officer or man. If he gets a married quarter he does not get the allowance except for approximately $10. The amount collected for rent varies from $51 for


a private to $103 in the case of a major, and there is not much difference, generally speaking, in the accommodation. I found recently in one Canadian city that they had a subsidized housing plan, assisted under the provisions of the National Housing Act, under which they were building 88 houses. The accommodation was about the same as our married quarters. However, the average rent was $41, with the lowest at $20, indicating an average lower than the lowest we charge private soldiers.
In addition to living accommodations there are operational buildings of all types, including depots, warehouses, workshops for all three services, as well as hangars and radar stations costing very large sums. Of the construction program this year we plan to spend roughly 30 per cent on living accommodation and the like and 70 per cent on operational buildings and services.
Obviously we must give the service personnel shelter and must provide this on a standard comparable to that they would enjoy if they were in equivalent positions in civilian life. It should be remembered that a good part of the service personnel spend a good part of each year living under conditions of considerable hardship, and virtually all of them are posted to another station every two, three or four years. This has a definite bearing on the type of accommodation and the scale of the furnishings provided. All this affects the morale of our armed forces. They must know that the treatment they get, the food they receive, the clothing they are issued and the weapons they use are as good as can be found. That is our intention. Everyone who has been in Korea or in Europe says that the morale of the Canadian forces is as high as it has ever been. I believe that is true also of the men in Canada.
We civilians, we people in parliament, can affect the morale of our forces. It must be remembered that this is a large operation. It is an effort by the whole people of Canada. Just think of it; we have in the armed forces, active and reserve, and their dependents, along with the civilians engaged in the work of the Department of National Defence; in those engaged directly in defence production, in defence industry or in support of those operations, just about a million and a half Canadian people or 10 per cent of the population of Canada. We are seeking in this vote an amount which represents about 10 per cent of the national income of Canada. Consequently it is right to say that this is an effort requiring the support of us all, indeed the support of all of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the policy of the government as far as national defence is concerned has been discussed on several occasions during the early part of this session. The minister called attention to the various debates which have been held. Only a few days ago a white paper was issued entitled "Canada's defence program 1952-53". Since very little new information has been given to us, either in the minister's remarks this afternoon or in the white paper, I do not intend to spend a great deal of time discussing policies upon which I have already offered my comments.
When the policy was outlined two years ago all hon. members supported the general principle of supplying strength in order to prevent aggression and playing our part by supplying such forces as were necessary under the United Nations agreement or under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to prevent the spread of aggression where aggression had already broken out. I think all hon. members realize today that we must continue our efforts in that direction.
The minister referred to the developments which have taken place in the two years since the outbreak of aggression in Korea, and he took particular credit to the government for the development in the strength, equipment and organization of our forces during that time. If it was necessary to make such a great effort during the last two years since the outbreak in Korea, it must be realized that the same government was in power and had in pre-Korean days allowed the defence forces of this country to sink to a position where they were far below the point which would provide reasonable security; nor were they in a state of efficiency or strength to enable us to meet such international obligations as we might be called upon to meet. In the pre-Korean days members on this side of the house called attention to the state of our defence forces. There had been a rapid demobilization of equipment and camps, a depletion of units and a failure to keep up training strength so that when the actual threat of aggression did arise there had to be a rapid semi-mobilization, the sudden bringing into force of hastily organized units and reconditioning of camps which had been allowed to fall into disuse, and the hasty transfer of personnel from shore establishments to ships and from one unit to another in order to have something ready.
This government had allowed the defences of the country to fall into a perilously low state and, as the minister said, it was not until then, and only then, that the government woke up to the necessity of providing adequate defences for Canada. What has been the result of this hasty speed-up to which reference has been made? We see
Supply-National Defence that in these quickly organized units there has been exceedingly heavy wastage of personnel compared with the numbers taken on strength. In the white paper tabled in the house a couple of days ago one finds that the total strength at March 31, 1952 was 95,394 and that during the previous year of 1951-52 the intake into the forces numbered 39,033 while the wastage was 12,066. The heavy wastage of one in three is indicative of the lack of foresight used in the hasty mobilization of such forces as were required.
Those of us who were members of the committee on defence expenditure realize that there have been exceptionally heavy losses due to theft, fire and other causes, losses which are costing the taxpayers of Canada many millions of dollars. In part that is also due to the speed with which it was necessary to build up our forces after the period of stagnation that had existed in the pre-Korean days. I am wondering whether we are really building up our forces along the right line. Are we not still building up our forces so far as their organization is concerned along the old traditional lines that have been in existence for many years? The minister used words to the effect that if war broke out today we would have to fight largely with the weapons of world war II. I can think of no more disturbing statement that could be made to the house eight years after the hostilities of world war II ceased.
With the threat of aggression today and the possibility of war almost around the corner, we are told that we would have to fight another war largely with the weapons with which we 'fought world war II. What concerns me even more is the fact that if we had to go to war today we should have to fight with very much the same organization we had in world war II. Have we really taken cognizance of modern trends? Are we really aware of the new concept of war today which consists so much of highly mobile hard-hitting units to which I have referred in the past? Surely the day of large formations of infantry soldiers is really past. The whole modern trend as visualized by modern military writers indicates that far more reliance will be placed on small, compact forces which are capable of being transported by air, are highly mobile and can be moved to any theatre of war.
A few years ago we heard a good deal of talk about the unification or integration of the various services. It seems to me we are drifting farther and farther away from the concept of a unified defence force. In the white paper to which I have already referred there is a discussion on page 5 of our contribution to the forces of the North Atlantic

Supply-National Defence Treaty Organization. We are told that the R.C.A.F. squadrons which are to be sent to Europe will be organized into an air division which is the air force formation normally adequate to provide air support for an army of four or more front line divisions. We are not relating our contribution as far as fighter forces are concerned to the contribution we are making so far as ground forces are concerned. We are supplying a ground force of one brigade, the 27th, to Europe; but so far as the air force is concerned we are making a contribution equivalent to the formation which would normally provide air support for four or more front line divisions.
We have not got four or more front line divisions. We do not plan to place four or more front line divisions in Europe; but it seems to me there should be some relation between the type of ground force and the type of air force that we are supplying. It seems to me we are still thinking in terms of world war I and world war II when we talk about the number of air force fighter squadrons which will support front line divisions.
Another indication of the additional expense which has been caused to the taxpayers of this country on account of the hastily organized forces is, in my opinion, this question of rotation. It has been found necessary to have this very expensive form of rotation; and it is very expensive if you are going to ship personnel across the Atlantic to Europe and leave them there for a period of only twelve months. For centuries the forces of Great Britain have been organized on the Cardwell system which provides for one regular battalion of a regiment to be stationed abroad and another battalion to be stationed in the United Kingdom, the two units being rotated periodically; but there never was such an extravagant form of rotation as that of transferring personnel of those units between the homeland and overseas every year.
Obviously the efficiency of the unit cannot be maintained with such rapid rotation of personnel; and though perhaps more men are gaining some experience, the unit cannot hope to maintain the same standard of efficiency as it would if there was a more extended period. Therefore I think the minister is wise to suggest that a change be made to extend the period of rotation, to somewhat reduce the enormous expenses which are now burdening the taxpayer; but I doubt very much if a period of an additional six months will meet the requirements.
The minister then referred to the question of the air force contribution to the
[Mr. Pearkes.l

North Atlantic Treaty Organization and indicated that the bottleneck might not be the actual raising of the personnel or the provision of aircraft but in the construction of airfields. That danger was brought to the minister's attention many months ago by the leader of the opposition who, at the last session of this parliament, called attention to the lack of technical troops in Europe and advocated the provision of engineer units which would assist in the construction of these necessary airfields in France and Germany. It is obvious that airfields are the most essential requisite for the efficient operation of any air force. We know that the airfields in France were largely destroyed and have not been rebuilt. Much of the big machinery which was available in France in pre-war days had been moved away into Germany. France suffered the experience of being an occupied power for many years and it would naturally take her some considerable time to once again build up her construction industry, which in France was faced with tremendous obstacles and with a tremendous task because there had been all the destruction of her cities and lines of communication. Those had to be restored in order to bring about an economic revival in France. That had to go on side by side with the reconstruction of military facilities which were essential for maintaining the forces of NATO, and it is therefore quite obvious that one of the first things that must be done before any R.C.A.F. component can work in Europe is to provide the additional airfields.
We are told there are to be two airfields constructed in Germany and two in France which will accommodate the twelve squadrons of the R.C.A.F. which are to be sent there. I believe that in this white paper the cost is mentioned as being somewhere in the neighbourhood of $22-7 million. That is a heavy expense to meet, and I wonder if there are not ways by which it might be reduced. I believe the paper mentions that the land for these airfields will be provided by the Republic of France but that the construction of the buildings, the construction of the landing strips and the general preparation of the airfield with all the necessary equipment will be paid for by Canada.
If that is so I cannot help feeling that Canada should approach the construction of these airfields along the most economical lines possible. If we simply tell the French government to go ahead and do the necessary work and we will pay for it, then we are not likely to have a very economical contract. It seems to me that if we are going to pay for this work we should have a good deal

to say as to how this work is going to be done, the type of machinery which is going to be used, and if necessary what firms are to carry it out. I do hope there are plans extant which will see that the construction of these airfields which are going to cost the Canadian taxpayers millions of dollars will be carried out in the most economical as well as the most efficient manner possible.
I say I think it is of the utmost importance that these airfields be constructed. In fact I would attach more importance to the construction of these airfields than to the dispatch of the actual fighter squadrons. I am not sure that it should be necessary for us to have all twelve squadrons located in Europe at one and the same time. I hope the minister will be able to tell us the causes which led up to the inclusion of the additional squadron and why that has become necessary, and will indicate the number of R.C.A.F. personnel who will actually be stationed in Europe. After all, it does not take very long these days to fly a squadron of jet planes to Europe. One sometimes wonders whether the actual stationing of those troops in Europe is essential. I have no quarrel at all with the provision of those squadrons, but I wonder if they could not get their training as efficiently here in Canada, where the facilities for flying are better than in Europe. Might that not be a sound reason for retaining some of these squadrons here?
I can see the advantage of having certain squadrons immediately available in Europe. I can see the advantage of certain personnel receiving training in Europe and becoming accustomed to flying conditions there; but we are placing practically all our eggs in one basket by sending by far the larger portion of our fighter aircraft and our trained air force personnel to Europe. We understand there will be a discussion on the various types available for such squadrons as remain here in Canada until such time as the CF-100 becomes available. I do not intend to discuss the question of policy at any greater length, because as I said before it has already been discussed.
I welcome the minister's suggestion that we deal with the estimates section by section as indicated in the details, starting off I presume with departmental administration and inspection. Before we go on to a detailed discussion, I should like to say a word of appreciation to the minister for the way he has accepted the suggestion which was made last year that more details be given in the pages of detail where, following the practice of other departments, the number of personnel in the various ranks has been set out. The only thing I think we might have had a little improvement in is the way in which
Supply-National Defence headings are given. It was much easier to follow the various headings in last year's estimates than it is in this year's estimates. For instance, the navy, army and so forth were set out far more clearly, enabling you to find the various items for the services more easily in the details last year than in the details as shown in this year's book.
You will recall, sir, that when we were discussing these estimates last year you called every item. I think if we are to have an orderly discussion of these estimates, without limiting the powers of the members to ask various questions, it would meet my convenience at least if these headings, such as defence services, administration, navy, army, were called instead of going down through all these minor headings such as civilian salaries and wages, civilian allowances and so forth as was done last year. I think that would not only assist the minister but would give all members of the house a wider range for questioning. It would not limit them quite so much. I have some questions to ask, so if there are other members who wish to discuss policy, I shall sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the procedure suggested by the minister, and as qualified by the member for Nanaimo, agreeable?
Agreed.

I am not going to make a long speech on the policy of the department, because earlier this session I made my stand abundantly clear. I should like to take just a few moments, though, and make some comments on the evidence brought out in the defence expenditure committee. Possibly the minister could make some reply later. I agree with the member for Nanaimo that the estimates of this department are much clearer and are put down in better form than they were previously. I agree with the minister that I think his department is wise in going rather slowly on orders for small arms until some measure of standardization can be attained amongst the various NATO countries.
I should like to mention briefly the fires and thefts that have occurred in the various establishments, as mentioned in the defence committee. I am not going to be critical at all, except to say that it appeared to me that in many cases the department was asking for trouble. For example the answers given to me in committee concerning 26 C.O.D. showed that in March 1950 the value of the building was estimated at $900,000 and the stores contained therein at $18 million. When the fire occurred in June, 1951, the stores were valued at $16,720,000. In January, 1952, the stores were valued at $23,850,000. It would appear to me that the average value
3648	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence of the stores contained in 26 C.O.D. would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $19 million.
The thing which struck me most forcibly during our investigations into the fires was the fact that, prior to the first fire and the recommendations made as a result of that fire, no sprinkling system had been installed and there was very little in the way of firefighting equipment. It would appear that in an establishment of this kind, where such tremendous sums of money were involved, every possible precaution against fire should have been taken. I agree that immediately after the investigation was made and recommendations were sent in, a good many steps were taken to eliminate the fire hazard in that particular building. But when we have a value somewhere in the neighbourhood of $20 million on the average, including the building and the stores contained therein, and particularly when no insurance can be carried, I would think every precaution should be taken at all times, and should have been taken before there were any fires whatsoever.
I did not have the time to dig into the various stores across the country, but I would imagine that very much the same condition could be found in all the various establishments that one might go into. I should like to know from the minister whether or not the same precautions and the same steps that are being taken at No. 26 C.O.D. and in some of the other places that we visited and investigated during the sittings of the committee are being taken in other parts of Canada.
I might suggest to the minister at the same time that even if it entails a little additional cost to the government or to the people of Canada, the whole thing might be speeded up. Those precautions might be instituted with a minimum of investigation, because in the long run we would probably save money, regardless of whether or not the thing were a hundred per cent perfect. We realize too that in the fall of 1951 a contract was issued to instal a sprinkler system in No. 26 C.O.D., which of course was after the second fire. I believe it is pretty well installed now. However, in my opinion it should have been done at the time the building was constructed.
I would not want to indicate that there is any doubt in my mind at the present time that they are doing everything they feel is possible to rectify the faults that are there. The point I should like to make is that in future, when any stores depot or other building that entails a lot of expense is constructed, all these fire protection devices should


be installed at the time of construction. If that were done we would save a whole lot of money, particularly in installation costs, if there were any fire at a later date.
Speaking generally on the theft situation, I do not want to make it appear that I think it is a bad thing. You are bound to find a certain amount of theft anywhere, whether it be in the service, in private life or in any kind of establishment. I know; I was in business myself, and used to lose the odd article out of the store. But I do think that in many instances the security precautions are not stiff enough. So far as No. 26 C.O.D. is concerned, for the life of me I have not been able to find out how anyone could take anything of any value out of there. Therefore any thefts out of there, particularly in recent times, are bound to be of a minor nature. But at the REME training camp at Barrie-field they have 1,216 acres. At the time of the thefts they had a security guard of only six men, which I think is entirely insufficient to cover a camp of that size, which would cover almost two sections. Perhaps the minister can indicate that these guards in the various establishments have been increased and that further precautions are being taken. I certainly hope so. I bring this to the minister's attention in the hope that he is considering some tightening up of the security regulations and some increase in the security guards. When the minister replies I hope he will tell us that that has been done.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish on a question of privilege to deal with something which was said yesterday at a time when I was not in the house. I might explain that it was necessary for me to be absent at a funeral at the time the hon. member for Coast-Capilano placed on record, together with certain statements which I do not propose to deal with in detail, one statement I feel should be corrected without delay. In his remarks, as reported at page 3568 of Hansard, which I did not have the opportunity to read when the house met this morning because it was not yet in my hands, I find that he quoted what purports to be a Canadian Press dispatch reading as follows, and referring to speeches I had made:
Speaking in French, he told audiences here, at Normandin, Mistassini and St. Felicien that family allowances should be increased, even doubled.

I feel sure, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano was well aware that this statement had been corrected. I noticed in the report that he had used some typically complimentary remarks about those who corrected press reports at other times. I have no doubt that his remarks applied to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and other ministers who have found occasion to make such corrections in recent months. In this case, however, I am not relying upon any correction of my own. The remarks I made were well and fully reported in UAction Catholique and Le Soleil which were represented at those meetings by reporters. They were in fact the only reporters present. The reports were accurate in every detail. They were based upon a written text which was strictly followed and which had been handed to them. I brought this to the attention of the Canadian Press when I saw their report on returning to Ottawa. I received a letter from the general manager of the Canadian Press, dated June 5, after they had an opportunity to inquire into the circumstances. That letter, in referring to this subject, had this to say:
We very much regret our inaccuracy and are issuing a corrective story for morning papers tomorrow.
I place that on record, Mr. Speaker, because the Canadian Press itself expressed its regret concerning this inaccurate report. I do not know yet what the source of that report was. There was no statement of mine made which by the greatest stretch of the imagination justified such a report. The papers which were represented there gave very full and very accurate reports, which indicated quite clearly that I had made no suggestion that family allowances be doubled. The Canadian Press very properly, and with the courtesy one would expect, after inquiring into the details, expressed to me their regret that they had on this occasion used an inaccurate report in their condensation of the dispatch they had received.

Mr. Speaker, the house will not be surprised if I say that I still feel this is not the place to be dealing with these divorce bills, being Bill No. 363 and Bills Nos. 367 to 389 inclusive, or any other divorce bills. I have taken that view with respect to the two or three hundred bills that have been put through the parliamentary divorce mill at this session. I am sure that in expressing that view with respect to these bills and the others that have gone through I express the view of a great many people in this country.
These petitioners having gone through the rigmarole which is associated with applying for bills of divorce, I would not regard it as being fair to them to delay them further at this stage of the session, and for that reason I am not objecting to the request of the hon. member for Lisgar that this batch of bills be considered for second reading under the one motion. But I repeat my insistence
(Mr. Winkler.]
that some day we must get divorce out of parliament.
Motion agreed to and bills read the second time.
