stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, June 20, consideration in committee of Bill No. 62, to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation- Mr. Larson-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, when Bill No. 62, to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation, was before the committee last Friday evening I took advantage of that opportunity to air certain of my own views. It just so happened that I was not given that opportunity until eight or ten minutes before nine o'clock, with the result that I was unable to conclude my observations during the time left to me. It was not my intention to talk out the measure, but it happened that I was speaking at the expiry of the hour allotted to private bills.
Last Friday I laid emphasis on the fact that what I was taking objection to was the procedure we follow in this house in granting charters to companies similar to the one we are dealing with at this time. I realize fully that objection to a company being granted a charter results in many cases from the conviction held by certain persons that gas or oil should not be exported from Canada. My personal view, as I have stated before, is that I have no objection, providing all the circumstances are as I think they should be, to the export of gas and oil from Canada.
I have indicated upon more than one occasion that I believe a province is justified in authorizing the export of gas and oil, particularly when it is concerned about seeing that the requirements of the people of that province are met as far as it is economically and physically feasible to do so. I would take the same attitude with respect to the export of gas and oil from Canada. I am fully convinced that when we contemplate the export of gas from Canada we should at all times be governed by the realization that as far as is economically possible the requirements of the Canadian people should be supplied.
If I were opposing this particular application for a charter on the ground that it might at some time engage in the export of either gas or oil, then in order to be consistent I would have had to do the same thing with respect to the other applications by companies Which have been before us and which might possibly eventually export gas or oil

from Canada. Once again I say that my principal objection is to the procedure for dealing with these matters.
I pointed out last Friday that for years we have held the view that such applications should not be dealt with by this parliament but by a semi-judicial body-we mentioned the board of transport commissioners-which should be given authority to do what we are presuming as a parliament to do at this time. I mentioned also that as long as we have applications from companies of this type coming before us, just so long are we going to find ourselves confronted with prolonged and protracted debates such as we have witnessed in connection with this application. In 1949 when the pipe line bill was being considered by a committee of the house we supported the idea that there should be a clause in the bill under which companies seeking charters would appear before a semi-judicial body, and that body could be the board of transport commissioners.
I rather fancy that much of the difficulty we have encountered in the house results from certain things which took place in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Regardless of what anyone may say, regardless of what defences may be put up, to me it is perfectly obvious that there was an effective effort to cut off the hearing of evidence in that committee. I have been a member of many committees during the past dozen years. Personally I have never encountered a situation before where I could conscientiously say there was an obvious attempt to cut off the hearing of evidence. I am afraid, however, there is sufficient evidence to indicate that that is what took place in this case. I think the chairman of any committee and the government majority on any committee would be well advised to go all-out to see to it that no room is left for a charge that the hearing of evidence was cut off. I also think it is wrong to refuse to hear witnesses where it is earnestly believed, not necessarily by the majority but by a substantial number of members of a committee, that other witnesses should be heard. If such requests are not granted then again it contributes toward a situation such as we have in this case. In fact I think it is bad policy to indicate almost arbitrarily when a witness is before a committee that so much will be heard from him and no more; and that was also done in this case.
I agree with a good deal of what the leader of the opposition said last Friday night. He pointed out that by granting a charter in this way we are automatically conferring upon the company broad, sweeping powers
Boundary Pipeline Corporation which become automatic as a consequence of section 7 of the Pipe Lines Act. That becomes particularly important when one realizes that very few of the members of this house, conceivably none, know exactly where the pipeline route is to finally go. I think of the powers of expropriation and the broad powers conferred upon a company under section 7 of the Pipe Lines Act. When one realizes at the same time that in the final analysis we have no idea at all where the pipe line is actually to run, then I believe we are taking upon ourselves a responsibility which as members of this house we should not have to bear.
I agree fully with the leader of the opposition, and as I stated last Friday night I think the government should initiate amendments to the Pipe Lines Act of 1949 authorizing the procedure I have outlined. The company would then appear before the board of transport commissioners. Witnesses could be heard and all relevant evidence procured. As a further safeguard there is of course the right of the province from whence the product, be it gas or oil, must come in the first instance before it can be transported to any other part of Canada.
Once again I want to emphasize that I am not trying to filibuster the bill. I am not saying what I am saying because of any personal opposition so far as the question of export is concerned. Certain recent developments lead me to the conclusion that if we desire to procure external markets, particularly for gas, we may have to hurry. I realize fully that possibly the province of Alberta is not in a position today so far as gas production is concerned to authorize a great many companies who apply for permits to export gas to do so at this time, but they do anticipate adequate reserves to enable substantial export. However, the thing that worries me a bit is whether, when we reach the stage where we have the required surpluses to export, markets will then be open to us for that product. I am not going to make any further observations at this time. I. hope the government will see fit to amend the Pipe Lines Act as I have suggested. I am sure the house would thereby be relieved of a heavy responsibility which I do not think belongs to this house. I think the whole matter could be dealt with in the best interests of the Canadian people by proceeding in that way.
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with considerable interest to what the hon. member for Red Deer has said-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps the hon. member will allow the hon. member for

Boundary Pipeline Corporation
Kindersley, who is the sponsor of the bill, an opportunity to speak. I see he has risen in his place.

Mr. Chairman, I know it has been said around the house from time to time that people have talked out their own bills, but in this case I see there are many others who are prepared to carry out that function and I feel I should be given an opportunity to say something on the bill.
I was approached some two years ago to sponsor this bill in the House of Commons. I considered the matter, and there were several points which immediately came to mind. One consideration was the fact that the proposed line was to go to Winnipeg. I probably felt that in going to Winnipeg it might not be serving the country to the best advantage. However, when I considered that the province of Alberta was obviously not prepared to be responsible for the amount of gas required to supply all Canada at this time, I felt some start should be made in supplying gas to the neighbouring provinces.
At the present time it would appear that the province of Alberta is not prepared to supply gas for export in any quantity until such time as the industrial development of Alberta based on a gas economy has been achieved. It is also quite possible that some considerable time could elapse before any major export from Alberta became a fact. It seemed to me that with this point in mind the province of Alberta might be prepared to make available for export a limited supply of gas much sooner than it would be prepared to be responsible for transcontinental supply. It seemed only justice to me that the very cold provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba should rate the same priority as Alberta's sister province of British Columbia.
In my opinion opposition to the bill has resolved around two major considerations. The first was put forward by the hon. member for Calgary West, who claimed that the economics of a line from Medicine Hat to Winnipeg were such that this parliament had no right to grant the company a charter. In his statement before the committee he made the point that he wanted parliament to make the final decision as to the economics of the line and in the process of making this decision a national gas policy should be evolved. He based his argument on the fact that the board of transport commissioners was too pressed with other matters to properly look into' all phases of pipe line development in Canada. On this latter point I submit that a change of government policy would be involved and, as such, I do not propose to debate the matter at this time.

As to the economics, I would suggest that this parliament is responsible first to see that the people financing the line are able to carry out their obligations if granted the necessary charter and the necessary permits. I think that point has been amply satisfied. Second, I submit this parliament should satisfy itself that the design engineers are competent to advise. That point should be amply satisfied because the engineers have vast experience in pipe-line construction in the United States; and if they are not competent to advise on this proposed company's operation, I do not feel that the advice is to be procured anywhere.
On the economic side I submit that if any money is to be advanced by any financial house their reputation will be ruined if they advance that money on an uneconomic proposal. After all, when the consideration of whether people are going to advance money on any proposition comes up, it is the financiers who finally settle the matter; and I say I think that point should be amply satisfied.
Then the hon. member for Calgary West stated that as yet he was not satisfied in his own mind-and I think quite rightly so- whether the eventual supply of gas to central or eastern Canada ' should properly come as an exchange with the United States or whether a pipe line across Canada was the solution.
There is another main point raised by those opposed to this bill. It is that if this line is built its eventual extension will be into the United States with no regard to the needs of those two great areas in Canada, first the lakehead and then central or eastern Canada. It has been mentioned that if this company is granted a charter it is horning in for nuisance value on somebody who has already been granted a charter to construct a trans-Canada pipe line; and that if it is granted a charter it will hold up that construction for many years.
It has been stated that this is a plot by the Fish Engineering Company to form a Canadian subsidiary to block us from ever having Canadian gas in eastern Canada. It was stated before the parliamentary committee that the Fish Engineering Company at present had no financial interest in the proposed Boundary Pipeline Corporation, and I think that statement can be substantiated.
Coming to the matter of the eventual extension of this gas line to the United States, a point which seems to cause great disagreement, I submit that in considering this bill that does not come into the matter at all because Western Pipe Lines has already been granted a charter to do the very thing these
[The Chairman.]

people are accused of intending to do. If that charter is already granted and the matter is already settled I cannot see how holding up this bill is going to satisfy any of the considerations which the opponents of this bill claim will exist. If gas is finally exported from Alberta in quantity I do not see how it is going to change the matter one little bit whether this bill is held up or not. The only thing that will do is give Western Pipe Lines a monopoly. I do not think that is Liberal policy, and I do not think it is the policy of others in the house who are opposed to this bill.
I feel that if gas can eventually be supplied to eastern Canada by a pipe line going across Canada on Canadian soil that should happen, and any person who has the interests of Canada at heart should think the same thing. I also suggest that the rule should not be so rigidly applied that gas would never be brought to eastern Canada or that it would be brought to eastern Canada at prices at which the interruptible industrial market could not buy it. I do not think that should happen at all. I believe the benefits of gas should be brought to eastern Canada by an all-Canadian route if that can be done. The hon. member for Calgary West said he was not sure that was the proper way to do it.
If we view this whole matter of the passing of this bill from a realistic standpoint, does it not all boil down to the fact that this company is merely asking for incorporation? It is asking for the right to become an entity so it can compete in a fair and equitable way with the people who have already been granted charters to build pipe lines.
Canadians have always felt, and history has shown, that much of our great advance is due to the fact that we have free competition in this country. Competition has demanded that the greatest economy be exercised so the producer gets the most for his product and so that the end consumer pays the least. I submit that principle applies here. By using this parliament to protect the interests of pipe-line companies already incorporated the Canadian public is being done a great disservice; and this parliament, in the way it is acting, is making itself a part and parcel of the disservice that is being done to the Canadian people.
If in the next year a supply of gas is available and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines is ready to build this line across Canada with ample finances and all the other requirements of the board of transport commissioners, it will emerge as the only company in the field. I have no objection to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines getting the eventual right to build that line; but what incentive will there be on the
Boundary Pipeline Corporation part of the people sponsoring that company, of the principals, to give the maximum price to the producer in the field and charge the minimum price to the consumer at the other end, because they will have a monopoly from the producer standpoint, and a monopoly from the consumer standpoint. On the other hand if the economy of this pipe-line development dictates that there will be reciprocal exchange of gas between Canada and the United States, and if the economics of it dictate that gas should be sent into the United States and brought back into Canada, Western Pipe Lines have a monopoly in that field. It might be all right to protect what would eventually become a monopoly; but it has never been the policy of the supporters of any Liberal governments in this country *-and those governments have been fairly successful-to support any monopoly.
I submit that if this parliament does its duty and allows any responsible group of individuals to incorporate themselves into a pipe-line company, the board of transport commissioners will be in a much better position to render proper judgment. That will be because every single company that appears before that board of transport commissioners will really have to ha^e its pencil sharp and get down to brass tacks, because there will be competition. They will have to get their economy to the point where' they are giving the absolute maximum to the producer of gas and charging the absolute minimum to the consumer. They will only be able to keep enough in the middle to carry themselves on an economic and proper business basis. The operating costs will have to be cut to a minimum, and the citizens of Canada will reap the greatest benefit. The board of transport commissioners can carry out this duty by giving the final go ahead to the pipe-line company which is prepared to pay the highest possible price and charge the lowest possible price at the other end. Instead of the pipe-line company being the master of the Canadian people, the Canadian people will be its master. That is the situation which I think should exist. I believe any fair-minded Canadian should be of the same opinion, because these companies are well able to look after themselves.
I want to refer for a moment to an issue of the Financial Post of June 14, 1952. The editorial on the front page is headlined "Ridiculous hold-up", and it reads:
Parliament pays lip service to reform of its procedures, but until it acts on this important cleanup and modernization, the house will often make nothing but a foolish spectacle of itself and important business will be neglected.
3654	HOUSE OF
Boundary Pipeline Corporation
That editorial goes on in the same vein for several paragraphs, and then it says:
Even more Important is the fact that even if Boundary gets the incorporation it wants, it can't do anything on its pipe-line plans without the sanction of the board of transport commissioners; a body much better equipped than the House of Commons to hear highly technical evidence and to allocate wisely route franchises.
It goes on to say:
Let them have their incorporation. Let the house get ahead with its work. Let the fight as to what Boundary does next be fought in the place provided for such bouts. '
I agree with that article. This is a paper which is highly regarded all over Canada. I do not see why this House of Commons should continue this business of holding up the normal incorporation of a company. The financial people can do the job. The engineers can do the job. I do not feel that any government in, Canada can sit by and watch something like this go on, thus protecting what will eventually become a monopoly. It will mean that one company will appear before the transport board and there will be, therefore, no competitive evidence upon which that body can base a decision. I submit the Canadian people will suffer. I believe this incorporation should be granted. I feel that we are doing the Canadian people a great disservice by carrying on in the way we have for the last few weeks.

I was pleased to allow the hon. member for Kindersley to take my place, Mr. Chairman, and I have listened to his remarks with considerable interest. At the outset I might say he has not convinced me that this house should pass the bill which is before us. Hon. members might ask why I, coming from the maritime provinces, should be interested in a pipe line which is to be constructed from Alberta to other western provinces. In reply to that, Mr. Chairman,
I think I can say that it is a general interest that we have as citizens of Canada. We consider that what is good for one part of Canada would be good for all of us.
We may be a little envious of Alberta which today has this great natural resource, of which we have none in our province. I might say also that our interest extends to the fact that when this Dominion of Canada was formed there were only four provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario. At that time we did have a great interest in the public domain of this country. These great natural resources which have been found in other parts of Canada were then part of the public domain, and at one time we did feel that we should have more than a passing interest in them.


This matter of the incorporation of a company, and the building of a pipe line, is a big problem. I feel that it would be a mistake for us, at this early stage of the development of this great gas industry in this dominion, to grant charters indiscriminately to every company making application. It might be said that all we in the parliament can do is grant the application, and that the feasibility of building and operating the pipe line could be decided by the transport commission. However, that is a chance that possibly we cannot take. Once we allow the matter out of our own hands we have very little control over the building of the line or the transportation of gas or oil. I did not have the opportunity of hearing the arguments before the committee which dealt with this matter. I was not a member of that committee. I have read certain of the arguments, however, and I have read the reports of the committee. I have listened also to the debate in this house on many occasions. We have had ample opportunity to listen to debates on pipe lines, not only on this bill but on many other pipe-line bills during the last two years.
From reading the reports of the committee, and also from listening to the debates in this house, regardless of what the hon. member for Kindersley has said this evening I am sure we must have some doubt as to the economic feasibility of constructing this Boundary transmission line. First there is the doubt raised in our minds by, the small size of the pipe line which is to be constructed, and also as to the advantages it is claimed will accrue to the people the line is intended to serve. Then there is a doubt raised in our minds, I think a very reasonable doubt, as to whether Canada should export gas until her own needs have been fully supplied. I believe that is a very important problem and one which we should carefully consider.
I have listened to applications for the incorporation of many pipe-line companies in this house, not only for gas but for oil as well. The thought has often occurred to me that if we granted incorporation to all pipeline companies requesting incorporation and those pipe lines were built, we would have pipe lines running in all directions across Canada. They would look like great snakes running from one end of the country to the other. I am sure that is something we should carefully consider. We all remember that in the early days when Canada was building railroads we were very careless and built more railroads per mile than this country required. Oil and gas transportation by pipe line is just another means of transportation, and I think we should carefully consider the

problem to ensure that we do not repeat the mistakes we made in years gone by. I agree entirely with the hon. member tor Red Deer when he says that somebody other than the parliament of Canada should deal with this matter of granting rights of incorporation in connection with pipe lines. I believe that body should be the board of transport commissioners. I have faith in the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, and I also have great faith in the Alberta government and in their good judgment to say what pipe lines should be built and what should not. I believe we can very well leave this matter to the consideration of the board of transport commissioners and the government of Alberta.
We know that the board of transport commissioners has also refused the Prairie Transmission company the right to build a pipe line down through British Columbia to the Pacific coast. We have heard that the Prairie Transmission Company Limited is also a subsidiary of the Fish Engineering Corporation, the same as the company which is now seeking incorporation.
There are three main problems which I have heard mentioned, and which should be considered. The hon. members from Alberta have stated very carefully that, as far as Alberta is concerned, the first consideration is to assure themselves that Alberta has all the gas it needs not only for the present but for some years to come. Since we are all Canadians, it does seem to me that our next consideration should be to see that Canada is preserving for herself a proper amount of gas, and that we are protected so far as the future is concerned. The third and last consideration should be what we are to do with any surplus we may have so far as exporting it to the United States is concerned. As I said, we are Canadians, and our first interest should be to see that the people of Canada are protected not only at the present time but in the future as well.
The hon. member for Kindersley sort of cast a little doubt on the quantity of gas that may be found in Alberta. If there is any limit to the supply, then definitely that limited supply should be saved for our own people. I think we could take a leaf from the book of the United States as far as this great asset is concerned. We have had ample evidence that the United States will not supply Canada until she herself has been satisfied. There is abundant evidence already on the record of this parliament to that effect. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Greenwood and many other hon. members have placed on Hansard the attitude of the United States government and the American
Boundary Pipeline Corporation people toward the export of gas. In that connection I should like to read from a report of the federal power commission in the United States relating to exportation. This case had to do with the application of Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line Company, dated April 12, 1946, to export gas from the United States to Canada near the city of River Rouge, Michigan, to be sold and delivered to the Union Gas Company of Canada, Limited. The judgment reads as follows:
No deliveries of natural gas shall be made to Union during the months of January, February, March, November and December in any year during the term of this authorization. Delivery of natural gas to Union shall be curtailed or interrupted whenever, and to the extent, required for the protection of deliveries of natural gas, either for immediate consumption or for storage, to any and all of applicant's customers in the United States. The authorization hereby granted shall not constitute ground or justification for any refusal by applicant to transport or sell natural gas to any person or municipality at any time during the time hereof, either for consumption in the United States by such person or municipality or for storage, or for resale for ultimate public consumption in the United States for domestic, commercial, industrial, or any other use, it being the intent of this authorization that at all times, persons and municipalities in the United States are to receive preferential service over that to Union.
As we all know, Union is a company in Ontario. That is a clear indication, Mr. Chairman, of the attitude of the people of the United States and of the authorities there to the exportation of gas from that country. There is other evidence of their attitude. As a matter of fact, in section 3 of their natural gas act they set out very clearly the attitude of the government of the United States to the exportation of gas from that country.
You do not blame them for that policy, do you?

Not a bit; I think it is a very wise and sensible policy. It is a policy that we should adopt in this country so far as the export of gas is concerned. Gas is not like our forests; it is not something that can be reproduced. Gas is a very expendable commodity. If we expend all the gas we have in this country in a few years in order to satisfy the people of this and the next generations, what are the people who come after us going to do? The policy adopted in the United States is to protect not only their own people at the present time-
Where does the gas come from with which you drive your car?
We can get a lot from you.

May I ask the hon. member a question? During the last war where did the gas come from that was used in his car?

Private Bills
The hon. member is talking about gasoline, and I am talking about another kind of gas altogether. If he would just pay attention-
Where does it come from?

As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, the gas that is found in Alberta is an expendable commodity. I was reading what the United States does in order to protect gas production. I am not speaking about gasoline, I might inform the hon. member for Charlotte.
It is all the same.

As far as gasoline is concerned, if they wish to protect that great natural resource for their own people and let our people have only what is surplus, they may do so. As I say, the policy of the United States is one that appeals to the people of the United States, and if it is a good policy for the United States I think it could be applied to the people of the Dominion of Canada in so far as the exportation of gas is concerned.
I move the adjournment of this debate.
You cannot do that.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 364, to incorporate the Canadian Shipowners Mutual Assurance Association.
Will the sponsor of the bill give an explanation?

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to thank the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) for his co-operation.
May I say at the outset that, while I do not want to dramatize this moment, it is only fair to tell hon. members that this is an historic moment in that it is the first time in Canadian insurance history that Canadian shipowners have banded together to form a mutual assurance association for protection against war risks in the event of a war breaking out.
The reason is very simple, and I shall make my explanation brief because I understand there is another bill to follow. Under present conditions marine insurance companies do not insure Canadian shipowners against war risks. The regular marine insurance companies in their policies usually have a 48-hour clause by which they may terminate any insurance covering a ship, in the event of the outbreak of war. Therefore the shipowner has two choices: (1) to leave his ship in harbour or (2) to negotiate a new contract with an insurance company at of course a greatly increased rate. The method of procedure in this instance is to form an association by which all the shipowners in Canada have the right to join a mutual non-profit association so that, in the event of war breaking out, they may have policies covering the value of their ships. These policies, in turn, are reinsured with the Canadian government which, it is felt, in wartime must assume the unnatural risk, if I may so describe it, of protecting private shipowners against losses from war risks.
The bill sets out the details as to who the incorporators are and the method by which they propose to operate this mutual benefit association. I think at this stage it would be wise to refer the bill to the committee on banking and commerce.

the second reading of Bill No. 365, to incorporate Ogdensburg bridge authority.
He said: Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as this bill should be non-controversial, and in the

light of the fact that it is to be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, I shall be brief in my explanation.
The purpose of the bill is to incorporate a company known as the Ogdensburg Bridge Authority. This company is to work in closest co-operation and conjunction vMth the bridge authority already set up by the house of assembly of the state of New York. I hold in my hand a copy of the measure passed by that legislative body.
There is a precedent for this bill inasmuch as it follows closely the legislation passed by this House of Commons to incorporate the Thousand Islands Bridge Company. The bill incorporating the company was passed in 1934, and there was an amending bill in 1936.
I might point out that the Prescott-Ogdens-burg Ferry Company is to be recompensed, as well as the land owners whose property must be acquired in order to complete proper approaches to the bridge. This bridge will conform to all the requirements pertaining to the proposed St. Lawrence seaway. Tolls are to be charged, and will be subject to the provisions of the Railway Act.
As in the case of the Thousand Islands Bridge Company when the bonds or other financial obligations are amortised the bridge will automatically become the property of the state of New York and Canada, the south half of the bridge going to the state of New York and the north half to Canada. In turn Canada, by order in council or otherwise, can designate to which province the bridge will accrue.
I do not think there is anything further to be stated about the bill. I do feel that the more bridges we have built, the more tourists will come to Canada, the better the Americans will know us, and the closer will be the bonds between our two countries. I urge that the bill be given second reading.

The committee is considering item 248 of the Department of National Defence. Shall we now begin consideration of the details of the vote according to the procedure agreed to earlier? These details
Supply-National Defence are to be found at page 289 of the estimates. I shall call the groups of details, subheading by subheading. Under this procedure, then, the first of these is, "defence services; departmental administration, including inspection services".
Defence services-
Departmental administration, including inspection services.

I notice an increase of $3 million in connection with civil staff. The white paper indicates that during the year there has been an increase in the strength of the armed forces from 68,426 to 95,394 which, roughly speaking, is an increase to the extent of about one third. But the increase in headquarters staff is practically doubled, namely from $3,393,842 to $6,024,852. I cannot help feeling that this is an indication of what has been described earlier in the debate as an inflated headquarters.
Would the minister be good enough to explain this large increase? I notice that as part of the increase there are additional assistant deputy ministers. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In connection with the increase in deputy ministers, there are two additional assistant deputy ministers: E. B. Armstrong, who was formerly with the treasury board, and L. M. Chesley, formerly vice quartermaster general. They were needed to cope with the increased activities of the department.
With regard to the increase in the civilian staff, almost all this increase is due to the increased activities of the inspection services which are in almost direct proportion to the amount of equipment orders that have been placed.
With regard to the proposed pentagon, I am sorry to say that we have not made much progress. There was some opposition last year which perhaps assisted in our not making any progress. We were unable to arrive at any position with regard to the location of

Supply-National Defence the proposed building. This must be undertaken at some future time, and the sooner the better, but it is not being undertaken now.
The additional amount for construction is in connection with a range for long-range artillery at Lake St. Peter amounting to $1,850,000, and magazines and power at Val-cartier, $160,000, making a total of $2,010,000.

speechtext: The personnel in the inspection services has just about doubled and the amount being provided for salaries is also just about doubled. What is the total increase in the civilian personnel covered by this particular heading?

They would all be civilian. No doubt the minister will recall that there was some question about the civilian personnel being increased from 30,000, which-was authorized a year ago, to 40,000. Are the salaries of those extra 10,000 provided for in this vote?

The minister cannot tell me the actual increase in personnel?

The increase in amount, not in number.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence

I just gave the increase in number, which is from 1,230 to 2,512. The increase in the amount would be $3,489,842 to $6,105,650 if you included prevailing rates and casuals in that category.

The minister said this afternoon that seven ships had been launched for the Canadian navy. Can he state whether any have been commissioned? If none has been commissioned, can he state when the first one will be commissioned and when he expects the last of the seven will be commissioned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: A number of minor vessels, such as minesweepers, are being commissioned this year, while others now under construction will not undergo their trials until late in 1953 and certainly will not be commissioned until 1954. I refer particularly to vessels such as the anti-submarine vessels, which are a totally new type. It is not possible to give dates because there may be all kinds of developments which will intervene. These are highly complicated vessels costing up to $15 million each and have never been produced before in any country. We aim at the highest possible production rate. We have seven on order and seven more to be ordered and we hope for the best.

Can the minister tell me how many of the ships that have been launched or are expected to be launched this coming year are small vessels, such as gate vessels, and how many will be anti-submarine vessels?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend a reference to page 18 of the white paper. We have commissioned one of the gate vessels, which is a ship. It is not an auxiliary vessel. Four are expected to be completed during the year. Of the fourteen minesweepers two were launched in 1951 and we hope they may be given trials this year. The patrol vessel Labrador was launched in 1951, commissioned in 1952 and we hope it will be ready for trials in the latter part of 1952 or in 1953.
I gather that the majority of those already launched or expected to be launched during the coming year are what you might call auxiliary vessels?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.
The anti-submarine vessels are not being launched at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Several of them are being launched this year, but the major part of our launchings this year will be minesweepers which are not auxiliary vessels. In connection with the naval shipbuilding program, we are now engaged on the current construction of 33 major vessels of four different types, the construction, current and immediately intended, of some 41 minor auxiliary craft of eight different types and the conversion and rearmament, in some instances to

the point of reconstruction, of some 40 major vessels of ten different types. It is a pretty complicated program.
I would take it that the minesweepers under construction are somewhat of a modified Bangor type which will be available not only for minesweeping but for escort duty to some extent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are minesweepers which can be made available to do the job that it is customary for coastal escorts to do.
Something similar to the Bangor?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is right, but much more modern in design. They are of entirely new construction with new equipment and armament.
I realize that.

Absolutely, Mr. Chairman. I should like to make one remark in connection with what the minister said this afternoon. He stated that the impression had gone abroad that the general world situation seemed to have improved. He went on to say that nothing, except one thing which I do not think he specified, would lead him to believe this general impression was correct. I should like to say I was extremely glad to hear the minister say what he did. I have been somewhat alarmed during recent months at the growth of what perhaps might be called a sort of ostrich view of affairs. In other words, the general opinion seems to have become rather current in the country during the last seven or eight months that everything is on the mend and that therefore the necessity for national defence was reduced.
I hope what the minister said in that regard will receive very wide publicity and will have a good effect in dissipating the view that the general world situation now is very much improved over what it was. In my view the events of the last two or three weeks particularly have confirmed that the general world picture is not only not better than it was but is possibly even worse. It
3660

Supply-National Defence seems to me that if the majority of people in this country get the idea firmly in their minds that everything is on the mend so far as the world picture is concerned they will also be convinced that the necessity for national defence is not very great and will not be prepared to support the defence effort one hundred per cent, which the minister indicated was absolutely essential.
I should also like to make some remarks with reference to the defence expenditures committee. I do not know exactly under what item of these details that might come. Possibly, Mr. Chairman, you might help me out of my difficulty in that regard so that when the appropriate item comes up I may say a few words on that subject. I shall leave it for the moment. So far as the defence objectives outlined in the white paper we received a couple of days ago are concerned, I think nobody in the house or throughout the country who has paid any attention to the matter has any quarrel whatever with them. We are all behind them one hundred per cent. Where any difference of opinion arises it is with respect to the means to be employed to carry those objectives into effect. In that regard of course I suppose there is bound to be a considerable difference of opinion.
I am still convinced, for example, that the expenditures on this particular matter we are dealing with, general administration, are greater than they need to be. I think the expenditures in regard to the equipping of our forces, training our forces, for accommodation provided for them and so on are greater than they need to be. That excess, if I may call it that, does not in my opinion contribute to a better and more efficient service but probably detracts from the efficiency of our defence effort.
I will say no more, Mr. Chairman, because I can see you are getting a little restive and I will address myself to one or two specific questions under this item. First, on these travelling and removal expenses, I see they are up from $290,500 to $910,000. These expenses of course have to do purely with the civil end of national defence headquarters, and I would ask why that very large increase is going to be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The two largest items in this increased amount are in the audit staff, $80,000, and inspection service travel cost, $760,000. Those two items account for practically the whole increase.
I am sorry I did not quite understand the minister's last statement. Do the inspection services account for $700,000 odd of that $910,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence

What does that mean exactly? Do you mean you have a large number of inspection personnel on the road?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes. We have virtually
doubled the size of the inspection service during the year due to the fact that the amount of equipment delivery has more than doubled, and a great part of the work has to be done away from the inspection service bases, which requires transportation.

Well, Mr. Chairman, as a matter of fact the next matter I was going to speak about was miscellaneous equipment for inspection services which for the year we are in amounts to $1,400,000 and last year was only $104,500. I presume what the minister was speaking about in regard to travelling expenses is the same with respect to this further item, and I would ask him what these inspection services are which have apparently been increased to such a large extent. I will refer particularly to miscellaneous equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence

Inspection what?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Gauges. This increase covers the purchase of inspection gauges for U.S. type equipment. The change-over to United States type guns, ammunition, etc. has made it necessary for the inspection service to reequip itself with inspection gauges. The bulk of the gauges the inspection service held before were those required during world war II for the manufacture of United Kingdom equipment.

I would like to ask one more question having to do with naval personnel. During the war we had two separate departments of communications which at that time were known as W/T, wireless telegraphy and V/S, or visual signal. Immediately after the war they consolidated the two into the communications branch. Something like a year ago I was talking to a lieutenant in communications and he told me they were considering transferring back to the dual system where they had the dual set-up as

they were having difficulty in handling both the radio end and the visual end, due to the difficulties of taking the signals,
I was wondering whether the minister could say anything about that, and whether or not they intend to continue the single communications branch or to again divide it into visual and radio as two separate branches, as they had been during the last war.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will have to look into the question raised by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. I think the general trend is for the visual system to disappear gradually, but beyond that I cannot go. I will have to get him the answer.

I might tell the minister that, being in the communications branch during the war, I found it very difficult to master both visual and radio for the simple reason that in visual signalling you read word by word and in radio you read letter by letter. When one accustomed to visual signalling tries wireless he has a tendency to read word by word, and when the situation is reversed the wireless signaller gets so far behind in visual signalling that he cannot catch up; in other words he starts to read letter by letter and cannot form words. I wonder if the minister knew anything about the matter, because from my own experience it is pretty difficult for anyone to try to master the two of them. Although the codes are the same, the methods of receiving messages are entirely different. I would like to get an answer at some later date.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will be glad to get that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Well, sir, the hon. member for Nanaimo has much more experience with transport matters than I have; also with the situation on Her Majesty's Canadian ships, particularly destroyers which he may see leaving from Esquimalt. There is not room on board one of those ships to put a single extra human body; they are loaded to full capacity of the ship. In order to use naval vessels for transport it would be necessary to put on special naval vessels. They are full of gear of all kinds and are very inefficient for the purpose of transporting troops, so except in most unusual circumstances are never used for that purpose. Our troops going to Korea are largely carried either in specially constructed troop ships operated by the United States navy or by air. While we have looked at other possible types of transportation, I am sure the way we are doing it is the most efficient and cheapest.
Are the naval ships as crowded as they were during the last war?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think some of them are even more so, because in the Far East we have to carry equipment, officers and men, sometimes staying at sea up to fifty days, so that vessels which did not carry certain stores or types of equipment now have to carry them. I think they are about as crowded as they were.
In other words, they get lots to eat.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence

They were used on the westbound trip to carry immigrants to Canada, and on the eastbound trips vacancies were used to carry the 27th brigade to Europe. That was done for a large proportion of the forces there, and we got very low rates indeed.

Can the minister tell me whether or not it is the policy now to have some sort of combined officer course such as

I was glad to learn, a few days ago from press dispatches, Mr. Chairman, that the government had at long last decided to pay the veterans of the Korean force the same clothing allowance which had been paid to veterans of world war II. About three months ago I brought this matter to the minister's attention, and it is encouraging indeed to members of the opposition to see that occasionally the government puts through much needed measures such as this, largely due to the pressure we bring to bear.
The matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention tonight is the need for combat pay for those who serve under fire in an active theatre of operations. Several months ago I asked the minister about this, and he replied that the Canadian forces serving in Korea were already receiving combat pay. Combat pay is very different from the overseas pay which the Canadian army in Korea is now receiving, and which is paid to
"Mr. Thomas.]

all servicemen who leave our shores for an active theatre of operations. Combat pay is extra pay which is given to those who serve in a special area, often under conditions of extreme discomfort and in constant danger from enemy fire and attack. The men who serve in the rear areas, such as clerks, artificers, driver-mechanics, motor mechanics and other tradesmen receive trades pay, which makes their pay higher than that of men of similar rank who do the actual fighting in the forward areas.
I believe the most important skill in any armed force is that possessed by those who achieve proficiency in handling their weapons under fire. I believe men who qualify in handling their weapons under fire should be paid combat pay in exactly the same manner as those who become proficient at their trade, and who are paid trades pay. I believe also that combat pay should be greater in value than any trades pay, because there is no skill in warfare that is comparable to that of handling weapons proficiently under fire. It is on that proficiency and skill that the outcome of any campaign depends. I believe that proficiency should be rewarded, with that importance in mind.
I would appreciate very much hearing the minister's comments on the need for paying this special kind of combat pay to those who become proficient in handling their weapons under fire while serving in an active theatre of operations.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
With regard to the first point, I can assure the hon. member that while his representations were given every consideration, the matter had been actively considered for perhaps six or eight months before he mentioned the subject.
With regard to combat pay, this involves a good many factors. We introduced a new type of tradesmen's pay last December. Under this, for the first time a trained infantry soldier became entitled to tradesman's pay for the first time. It is our view we should not go beyond that. We are paying a special allowance to men serving in the field. Our rates of pay are as good as any; the rates of pension are better than any and the treatment we give is as good as any we know about. We think that, taking into consideration the traditional practice of those serving in the British armed forces of trying to deal fairly with all men and all ranks, this is about as far as we can go at this time.

I should like to ask the minister specifically, does he consider that the skill required to handle a rifle, machine gun or Bren gun under fire against an advancing enemy, which after all is the skill upon which depends the success of any campaign, should

be less highly paid than that of the man who serves in the rear areas in comparative safety and comparative comfort at a trade such as clerk, artificer, motor mechanic or driver-mechanic, or one of the many other trades that receive trades pay? I have no objection to these men receiving trades pay. I think they deserve it for their proficiency. My whole contention is that the highest skill in any armed force is that of the man who handles his weapons proficiently under fire, because if he falls down the whole campaign falls down and all the tradesmen in the rear areas are simply mopped up by the enemy. I claim that the highest trade, the highest skill, should be paid higher than anything else, and I believe there is no problem in qualifying a man under battle conditions as being a man who can handle his weapons proficiently under fire. To me it is most important that that skill should be rewarded. Will the minister answer that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is the case today.

Can the minister say specifically what a private who is a Bren gunner in a forward platoon receives per day as compared with a motor mechanic or an artificer? Will he give me that answer in the daily rate of pay?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That was given in a release of the department in December when this new basis of pay was extended to qualified soldiers in the infantry and other formations. The qualifications and the rates are similar for all trades.

I am afraid that is not an answer at all. I have asked the minister the question, and I should think he would be familiar with these figures. I am asking him whether all trades pay is the same? It must be simple to give me the figure for the private who receives trades pay, and it must be simple for the minister with his knowledge to give me the figure of what the private-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not carry these in my head. I can assure the hon. member that he flatters me when he suggests it; but the monthly rates of group pay for the tradesmen in addition to the monthly rate of pay set out for the rank are as follows: group 1, effective October 1, 1946, $4; effective December 1, 1951, $6. Now for the first time, subsequent to the introduction of this order effective December 1, 1951, the trade groupings were extended to infantry soldiers as well as others, in addition to what were ordinarily called tradesmen before.

Can we get right down to figures? The minister has his deputy minister and another official from his department in front
Supply-National Defence of him. They ought to have these figures. They must know the figures I am asking for. I am asking specifically, what does a private who serves in the front line under fire, handling a Bren gun, receive and what does a private who serves in the rear areas as an artificer or a motor mechanic receive? These are two specific questions. The minister has all that information in front of him, and he must be able to answer me.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It all depends. Surely I must have made myself clear to the hon. member. I ask hon. members if I have not. If he is entitled to trades qualifications, either as an infantryman, an artilleryman, an artificer or a driver, then he will get in addition to the ordinary pay of his rank, if he falls into group 1, $6 per month.
