Does that apply to a man who handles a Bren gun in the forward area?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If qualified as a tradesman according to the rules laid down for an infantry soldier.
But, Mr. Chairman, I asked whether a proficient Bren gunner, a man in a forward platoon, qualifies as a tradesman if he is simply a Bren gunner or a rifleman.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Right.
If he be proficient?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Right.
Then he gets his $6 in exactly the same way as the motor mechanic gets his $6 extra?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; that is if the motor mechanic is a trained tradesman according to the standards laid down in the army service corps for motor mechanics.

Since we appear to be on rates of pay there are two or three questions I should like to ask. Looking at page 12 of the white paper which was recently issued I see the rates of pay for various ranks, but I see nothing there in regard to rates of staff pay. Can the minister tell us what the rates of staff pay are at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is no staff pay.
There is no staff pay whatever at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.
Is there anything equivalent to staff pay as we had it during the last war?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Could we have another question while I verify that? My recollection is that there is none. There might be some categories of what is called responsibility

Supply-National Defence allowance which might fall within the category my hon. friend is asking about, although there is no staff pay as such any longer.

Is that true of the whole service? For example, does the brigade major of the 25th brigade in Korea receive the same pay as, we will say, the major in command of A company, second battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry receives?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: He receives in addition overseas pay, and because he is serving in an active theatre of war he receives an allowance in respect of income tax, which is quite substantial.
No; I think the minister has misapprehended my question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: He does not receive any extra pay on account of his appointment.

Perhaps I have not made it clear. I will phrase it again. The first battalion of the P.P.C.L.I. is now in Korea. My question then would be this. Does the brigade major of the 25th brigade in Korea receive exactly the same pay as the major in command of A company of the 1st battalion P.P.C.L.I., which is also in Korea, receives?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is right.
Does the minister consider that the brigade in Europe today is on active service in the same way as the brigade in Korea?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, not the same. He does not receive any allowance in respect of income tax, or for overseas service.
I misunderstood the minister. In answering the last question I thought he said that the major in Germany today would receive overseas pay and active service pay.

I have one or two other questions on pay and then I have some other questions on other matters. The next one in regard to pay is this. Are our paratroopers in the 1st battalion P.P.C.L.I. and the 1st battalion R.C.R., and the Royal 22nd Regiment who have now been sent to Korea to be cut off from their jump pay when they are posted to Korea?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In order to continue to be qualified for the paratroopers' pay they have to belong to a jumping unit and $30 a month is paid while undergoing flying or parachutist training, or while filling a role requiring active or continuous flying. There are regulations laid down to require that in order to continue to qualify for this pay for these operations, they must take part in a certain number of operations within each period.
As I understand the minister's answer it comes to this, that when a paratrooper is posted to Korea his jump pay is cut off; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If he is posted to an infantry unit which is not doing paratrooping, he loses his risk pay. But at the same time, having been posted to the 25th Canadian infantry brigade in Korea he becomes entitled to overseas pay and also to the income tax allowance, which may be more valuable.

All I want is an answer yes or no. I take it from what the minister has said that his paratrooping or jump pay is cut off when he is posted to Korea. I presume the same thing applies if he is posted to the 27th brigade in Germany?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Answering an earlier question:	As I suspected, there is one case of
responsibility allowance, and that is for officers appointed as adjutants, who receive $15 a month extra.
Adjutants?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, adjutants. Doctors and dentists receive an additional $60. Risk pay is paid with respect to continuous exposure to risk. Once that exposure concludes, the entitlement to that pay ends. But on the other hand, upon being posted to Korea, the officers and men become entitled to both the overseas allowance and the allowance in respect of income tax, which in most cases is at least as high as if not higher than the other amount.

I should like to ask one or
two further questions with regard to pay. Does the minister know how many members, if any, on the staff at national defence headquarters here, and on the staffs of commands, are still drawing jump pay?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No. I would be glad to have any such cases drawn to my attention.
I am not drawing any case to the minister's attention. I am asking him how many, if any, in those categories are drawing jump pay.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not know of any.

The minister says that any paratrooper assigned to an infantry group and sent to Korea is deprived of his jump pay. In the event that any such paratrooper were called upon or volunteered to jump into enemy territory, how long would that jump pay continue, or would it be of very short duration, added to his ordinary pay he would receive overseas? Would it carry on for a month, or any stated length of time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Except in most unusual circumstances of a rather hush-hush nature-

and we would not expect this to develop- they would be attached to a paratroop unit, and then would be entitled to risk pay. It is the attachment to the paratroop unit and the exposure to risk which creates the entitlement to the risk pay.

In other words if a man were a paratrooper and assigned to front line duty in Korea he would not receive his jump pay; but if he were assigned to a paratroop group behind the lines in Korea he would not only draw his overseas pay, but he would also draw his paratroop pay, whether or not he made any jumps.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That has not happened.
But it could easily happen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If we had a paratroop unit, taking part in activities in Korea, and if such a man had proceeded from an infantry battalion to a paratroop unit which was taking part in paratroop activities in Korea', then he would be entitled to the risk pay.
That is complicated enough for me.

Purely as a matter of interest-and I cannot help being interested in the difference between a stafE officer and an adjutant, having served as both myself-I should like to ask a question. I entirely approve of doing away with staff pay, but I am interested to know what the distinction is between an adjutant and a brigade major. I am not objecting to it, but I am just interested to know.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The hon. member was a major himself, as I remember it, in the first world war. He will recall that normally an adjutant in a unit, as I understand it, is a captain. For his rank he carries more responsibility and a heavier burden than is carried by the ordinary captain, but rather less than was carried formerly by the major.

I think that certainly a brigade major carries a great deal more responsibility than a major who is a company commander or a battery commander. I do not think the minister's argument holds good at all. If there is a differential between the second in command and the adjutant, then there is the same differential between the company commander and the brigade major. What is the explanation of that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The major, whether in a brigade or a company, is receiving $335 a month basic pay, whereas the captain would receive $255 basic pay; and that is a pretty big differential.

But what the hon. member for Greenwood and I are getting down to is this.
Supply-National Defence We do not care which way it is, but we think it should be the same all the way through. There is the same differential in responsibility between the captain who is second in command of a company and an adjutant as there is between the major who is company commander and the brigade major. Why should the adjutant get extra pay over a captain who is a company commander, while a brigade major, who has the same increase in responsibilities, receives no increase over the company commander or the battery commander? What is the answer to that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Because the captain gets very much less pay than the major to begin with. And if the captain is doing work which is considered equivalent to that of a major, then it is considered that should have some extra recompense for his extra responsibility, whereas the major seems to be adequately paid anyway.

I was rather interested in the first part of this white paper, which deals with the first objective, so far as our defence is concerned, and that is defence against direct attack. It goes on to speak of radai installations, fighter control and the like, but it makes no mention whatever of antiaircraft defence.
In previous years I have referred to what I have considered to be a severe deficiency in respect of our anti-aircraft defences. Why is no mention made of anti-aircraft defence, and what provisions are there in existence, or being projected, for this type of defence?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member raises on this occasion, and has raised formerly, one of the most controversial and difficult questions we have to face. We have a large number of anti-aircraft batteries in Canada. I do not want to say, any more than the hon. member would, anything that would indicate that they are not important, because the fact is that I regard them as of the greatest importance. But the fact is that in connection with anti-aircraft guns and anti-aircraft warfare we are in one of these transitionary periods where we are moving from the heavy and light anti-aircraft gun, particularly the heavy which existed at the end of the second world war, into the field of guided missiles. How soon that will come we do not know. How profitable it is for us to spend the amount of defence dollars necessary to have anti-aircraft forces, either in being or ready to be brought into being, is difficult to say in view of the prospect that there will be something quite different which will be far more effective within two or three years.
I have spoken with extreme frankness because the hon. member has raised the question. I think he knows the answer. This

Supply*-National Defence is a question of great difficulty. We must have anti-aircraft batteries, both light and heavy, in the number that we have. They are equipped, subject to some modifications by way of fire control instruments and the like, with as good equipment as there is available; but how much further we should go into the modification of anti-aircraft guns in the light of anticipated developments is difficult to decide.

I must say that the minister has ascribed to me much more knowledge than I possess when he says I know the answer. I know very little about it. As he knows, I have been disturbed for a considerable time over our ack-ack defences and what ack-ack defences we are projecting. I must say that the minister's remarks have thrown a certain amount of light on this matter.
He said we have a large number of ack-ack batteries in Canada, but I know he must refer to reserve force batteries. There is no reason why I should not say that there are few permanent or regular force ack-ack batteries. There is no reason for not saying, because it has been said by many other people, that the reserve force ack-ack batteries have not their full complement of guns or anything like it, and they have much less than their full complement of men. To say that there are large numbers of ack-ack batteries in Canada does not mean a great deal from the defence point of view because those ack-ack batteries are not in a position where they could go out and defend targets.
The importance of anti-aircraft defence was impressed upon me strongly as a result of a trip I took with a large number of members over the week end to the industrial area in Quebec lying up from the head of the Saguenay river. It struck me forcibly that if there was any place in Canada that needed ack-ack defence, it was there. I know there are numerous other industrial areas which need it just as badly.
I know what the minister has said with regard to guided missiles is of extreme importance. I assume that along with our allies we have been doing considerable research in air-to-air guided missiles, rocket weapons and air-to-ground weapons. It is important to know how long we will have to wait to get into operation batteries of air-to-ground rocket weapons, and whether in the meantime we should not have in operation or existence the regular form of ack-ack weapons as we have known them in the past. I do not know whether the minister would care to elaborate on what he said before, but I would like to have his views as to what is

proposed immediately as far as anti-aircraft defence is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
At the present time we have the guns to make a defence. Some of those guns are being modernized up to the latest standards. Our experience has been that to modernize such a weapon may not produce that margin of difference between what it was before and what it will be afterward which would justify the expenditure, in view of the fact that we expect that in three or four years there will be a much better weapon available. The cost of modernizing equipment of this kind is quite heavy indeed.
We are doing about one quarter of our guns, and we have a considerable number. Frankly we are hesitant about expending money in doing the rest in view of the time involved, and also when it is considered that the cost of modernizing each gun, despite the fact that the difference between what it was before and what it may be in the future is marginal, is about equivalent to the cost of a modern fighter. Our thought is that it is better to have more modern fighters than more heavy anti-aircraft guns in view of [DOT] the fact that all anti-aircraft guns, especially heavy anti-aircraft guns, are expected to become obsolete within a limited number of years.

I certainly agree with the minister that it is preferable to have a modern fighter than to modernize a last war antiaircraft gun. Have any steps yet been taken or is it proposed to take them shortly to convert present ack-ack batteries into air-to-ground rocket batteries?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have no rockets yet. Experiments along these lines are being carried out in other countries and we are prepared to follow their experience. It should be very easy to catch up with them. I think the experience of all gunners is that it is possible to adapt themselves rapidly to new type weapons. For example, our gunners were able to use 105's or 25-pounders, and similarly during the first and second world wars our gunners quickly adapted themselves to the use of new type weapons. I am sure they will be able to adapt themselves quickly in the future to rockets.

Since the question of antiaircraft defence has come up I should like to ask the minister a question which he need not answer unless he thinks an answer is desirable. Has there been any hesitation in developing in Canada newer weapons such as the ground-to-air homing rocket, which has such a great potential for air defence, and the new air-to-air weapon which is colloquially known as the fabula and which

apparently is a fragmentation homing weapon? I mention this because it is common knowledge, having been mentioned in the press, that these homing weapons have had outstanding success.
It seems to me that nothing would be more desirable for air defence than to concentrate on these new weapons. There is nothing secret about these things, as they have been referred to in the newspapers in the United States, in the technical journals of the United States air force and in our own journals. I realize the minister's difficulty in this regard, but I hope he can make a statement to the committee that something is being done along this line so we will at least have the protection of the most modern weapons available.
That brings me to the other question, and it is one of enormous difficulty. I refer to the standardization of ammunition. At the present time there are no less than five different calibres of small arms ammunition, and if you count the -50 Browning machine gun as a small arms weapon there are six. There may be more, but those are all I know of. There is the -280 of the United Kingdom, -300 of the United States, -303 of the United Kingdom, -450 of the United States, -50 calibre of the United States and the 9 millimetre which I gather is common both to the United States and the United Kingdom.
I realize that no problem has given the minister a greater headache than the standardization of arms, and there is no problem more important to us in Canada. It is not so much a question of standardizing the arms as standardizing the munitions because if, unfortunately, we have to fight, we will be fighting in association with groups of people who are already armed with various types of small arms to which their troops are accustomed. The situation presents difficulty as instanced by the prejudices of our own troops in Korea based on fighting experience for the rather old-fashioned Lee Enfield in preference to the more modern Garand rifle. It is a tremendous problem and the minister is beset with great difficulties, but it is no use for us in the house to say that we are faced with an impossible situation.
We have two warring factions, one favouring the United States type of ammunition and the other favouring the United Kingdom type of ammunition. The great challenge is to do everything we can humanly do to see that the types of ammunition, particularly for the same arms, are standardized. Even though the type of arm may vary from country to country we should try to see that the ammunition is useful and applicable to all arms.
Supply-National Defence I know it is easy to get up in the House of Commons and say that is the goal. I know it is easy to say we should do this. I realize the difficulty, but I think it would be helpful to the committee if the minister would make a statement tonight on the problem of standardization of small arms.
I know it is one of the supreme headaches today in all armies; but I think the more we talk about it, the more we discuss it, the more it is brought out into the open, the more likely we are to find a solution. This is not a hush-hush problem. It is not a conflict between the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. It is something that must be worked out with the good will of all concerned. I bring up the matter knowing it to be controversial, knowing it to be a headache, knowing it to be a problem that must be faced, merely to give the minister the opportunity to state his opinion, if he so desires, because I feel we in Canada occupy a unique position in this regard. What I am saying to the minister is not said in any critical way. It is said entirely to be helpful, because one of the great problems the United States has to face is the standardization of ammunition. I feel that no country occupies such a key position as Canada in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member for York West brought up two questions. The first had to do with the position regarding guided missiles and the second concerned small arms and their ammunition. With respect to the first, it is a field in which most of the work of research is being done in other countries at the present time. I can assure him that hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent on it. In defence research and in the armed forces we have limited ourselves to keeping up with the progress in development, and also we have undertaken research in one special field, that of air-to-air missiles. We are doing special work in that field.
With respect to small arms, I am very glad indeed to have his encouraging words in support of the position I took this afternoon when I expressed the same view.

There is another entirely different matter I wish to raise. I am sorry I was not in the house to hear the minister but I was attending a committee dealing with a subject which was at one time controversial. I hope there can be established in our armed services the counterpart - of what is known in the British army as NAAFI, the navy, army and air force institute. I have had the privilege of visiting several military camps in the past year. The training officers as well as those on the G side in those camps complained to me that a great deal of the time

Supply-National Defence of training officers, who had duties elsewhere, was taken up with the auditing of the accounts of the camp grocery or department store. People were telephoning the colonels, regimental commanders, adjutants and others saying that they had brought a tin of such and such at the camp grocery and it was no good. This may seem a comparatively small matter, but when one considers that in some of our large military establishments the gross turnover in these stores runs to well over $1 million or $1,500,000 a year I think it is most unfair to ask regimental officers who are dealing with the training of a unit, or camp officers who are dealing with administration in a major military camp, to deal with the petty irritations occasioned by the bookkeeping of the camp grocery store.
I would hope, Mr. Chairman, that some consideration would be given to the establishment of an organization such as is known in the British army, the United Kingdom service, as NAAFI. I know we may have had criticisms of NAAFI overseas. We may have thought NAAFI coffee was pretty poor and we may have had other criticisms of it, but the establishment of such an organization takes off the shoulders of your training and technical officers-your G officers, your A officers, and your Q officers-the frightful irritation of running grocery stores and department stores and all other civilian operations which go therewith.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member for York West has recalled to my mind an answer I should have given to the hon. member for Broadview. There is additional pay given to an adjutant as a responsibility allowance partly in consideration of his having to handle the funds for the regiment which, as the hon. member says, is quite a burden.
With regard to the institution of NAAFI or something equivalent in Canada, we have had the matter under consideration for quite a long time. There is a lot to be said for it. The main thing to be said against it is that it removes from the local unit, whether it be a ship, army unit or air station, the interest and incentive that assures efficient manage

nent and local interest through local control if the funds created. Those two things have to be balanced and as usual there are differing views, but all are being considered.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the section carry?

On page 4 of the white paper which was issued, under army I see:
The army is continuing to maintain a mobile striking force for defence against a surprise airborne attack.


During the past two or three years the minister has always referred to our armed force for defence against airborne attack as our "airborne brigade". Why is it that here in the white paper and in the speech made this afternoon there was no mention of the airborne brigade at all? What we had mentioned was a mobile striking force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is essentially a brigade. The name was changed but I do not remember when, though I think it was about two and a half years back and "mobile striking force" is the term that has been used ever since.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the section carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. We were still using the term "airborne brigade" last year when we were discussing the estimates. Whether it was changed as far as army nomenclature is concerned, I do not know. It appears to me that the reason it was changed, and I think rightly changed, is that we no longer have an airborne brigade. Our airborne brigade essentially has gone to Korea, and the people who have had training in Korea and have come back from there have not yet been trained as airborne or parachute troops. I do not think they are any worse troops, and I think probably their experience in Korea makes them more effective fighting troops than they otherwise would be. But the situation, I would take it, is that we no longer have an airborne brigade and therefore the term has been dropped.
There is another point in the white paper under army which I would like to ask about. It is mentioned on page 18 under army equipment that:
Deliveries on orders of U.S. army equipment are proceeding. First deliveries from Canadian production of U.S. pattern equipment are anticipated in the last quarter of 1952.
In view of all the evidence we had in the defence expenditure committee that appears to me a very peculiar sort of paragraph. As I understand it United States orders have already been delivered. With respect to deliveries of Canadian production of United States pattern equipment being anticipated in the last quarter of 1952, I would like to ask the minister what United States pattern equipment it is anticipated we will be turning out from our factories in 1952.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the first point and the hon. member's suggestion that we have ceased to have an airborne brigade which we had before, I can assure him that is not so. The change in terminology has no reference to the strength or composition of the forces. The terms "brigade" and "mobile

striking force" were used the year before last and last year according to my recollection, and there is no change in the constitution or the composition of the forces. We have the three battalions and the other elements that we always had.
With regard to delivery of United States equipment, we have been quite frankly disappointed in deliveries but that was due to circumstances over which we had no control and over which we do not think the United States had any control either. We have never said that we had delivered to us all the United States equipment that we expected. Events have prevented it, and we will get deliveries as the equipment becomes available. In the meantime we are undertaking the manufacture in Canada of 105 mm. guns and ammunition, 155 mm. guns, and various types of mortars and the like. That is proceeding. The 155's will be coming off the production line later this year and so will the 105's. Ammunition for the 105's is about to be produced in considerable quantities, I understand. That is the job of my hon. friend the Minister of Defence Production. The principal two items that we planned to get from the United States and on which deliveries have been suspended are tanks and small arms and the reasons for that have already been given.

I do not want to enter into a controversy with the minister over the question of whether the mobile striking force is the same as it was before or not, but I do not think there is any question that it is the same or anything like the same. The term "airborne brigade" is no longer used, no longer appropriately used, because of the fact that the airborne brigade which was trained as such is now serving in Korea. The second battalions of the regiments which formed that brigade are in two cases just back from Korea. The members in most cases are still on their leave and are not back to receive training as airborne troops. There is no question but that the result is that we have not an airborne brigade at the present time and we will not have one for some months, under the very best of circumstances.
As I say, I do not want to enter into a controversy with the minister over that point, but I would just like to make that statement in explanation, considering what he said a few minutes ago.

I wanted to ask the minister a question about the equipment of the 25th brigade in Korea, which I think comes under this item of armoured fighting vehicles. As I recall it, last year when we were discussing the estimates, or very shortly after the 25th brigade was sent to Korea, we were discussing whether or not that brigade should be accompanied by a squadron of tanks, and we

engaged in a controversy with the minister as to whether anti-tank guns should be properly classified as armoured fighting vehicles or artillery. The minister told us at that time that all that was being sent over were anti-tank guns. We recommended that the brigade should be accompanied by a squadron of tanks.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the decision of the minister as announced at that time that they should not have tanks was reversed within about three months from the time this brigade arrived in Korea. Is that correct or not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would have to refresh my memory on the details and dates. The fact is that the brigade went to Korea with the type of weapon which was considered suitable for it, which was 17-pounder self-propelled guns mounted on tracks, a tank chassis, which the hon. member I think at the time called the tank, but that was not the name given by the Canadian army.
No, indeed; I said anti-tank guns.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I forget what the details were, but there was some controversy as he says. Anyway, it is a tank chassis carrying a 17-pounder gun. Some people call it a tank; some people do not call it a tank, but call it an anti-tank gun.
When this unit arrived it was found that in order to have additional fire power and also for greater uniformity these should be replaced by the United States Sherman M-4 A-3 EH tank, which was very similar to these Sherman tanks we have in Canada but with later modifications. That was done, and the 17-pounder anti-tank guns on their self-propelled tracks were made available to and went to our North Atlantic treaty allies and have since been delivered. There is no mystery about it. It was done in accordance with the views of the army; it has worked out satisfactorily, and we do not know why there should be any fuss about it.

The reason there should be some fuss about it is this. If the minister will look back at the discussion which took place in this house on his estimates, when the sending of the 25th brigade to Korea was being discussed, he will find that various members on this side, particularly including the hon. member for Calgary East and myself, suggested the brigade should be equipped with tanks. We raised a very specific question as to whether it was advisable to send that brigade over there without armoured fighting vehicles to support it.
Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: These were armoured fighting vehicles.

Well, we raised specific questions as to whether they were adequate. We said, in our opinion, that they were not; that they should have tanks. I raise this question at the moment because it appears to me it has been proven by the experience of the brigade in Korea that the decision should have been taken in fact at the time the brigade was sent.
We have often heard in this house and in this committee criticism on the views put forward on this side. I am not attempting to say that we are always right and somebody else is always wrong. We have been advocating for some time as a policy, both with respect to the brigade in Korea and with respect to the brigade in Europe, that there should be more concentration on armoured fighting vehicles, that is tanks, in support of infantry. Indeed, with respect to the brigade in Europe, I know the hon. member for Nanaimo, the defence critic for the opposition has suggested that instead of concentrating so much on infantry we should concentrate on armoured formations.
The point I want to make is that it does seem to me that, based on experience in Korea, that criticism appears to have been fully justified. It seems to me the experience in Korea has demonstrated not only that the criticism was justified but that the decision of the military forces, which I presume was backed up by the minister, resulted in expenditure of a very considerably larger sum of money to acquire tanks on short notice to support the brigade in Korea than would have been necessary had the suggestions made by this party been adopted at the outset and tanks acquired and sent over with the brigade to Korea when they went.
The reason I make that statement is that we have an answer which was given to a question asked in the defence expenditures committee which shows that 20 M-4 A-3 EH Sherman tanks were first acquired for the 25th infantry brigade in May, 1951. One was subsequently acquired for the 25th reinforcement group for training reinforcements in June, 1951, and that was almost immediately after the brigade landed there. My recollection is that evidence was given in the defence expenditures committee that the cost of these Sherman tanks, particularly having to be acquired as they were on short notice, was considerably in excess of what it would have been had we acquired other types of tanks, particularly the British Centurion, and placed the order at the time it was being urged on this side of the house that we should concentrate more on armoured fighting vehicles.

Mr. Speaker, one of these reports recommends the introduction of a bill to establish a pension fund. Hon. members will recall that when giving notice of the motion to set up a committee I stated that if there was such a recommendation it would not be apt to meet with objection on the part of the government, but that any bill would have to be preceded by a resolution and the necessary constitutional recommendation to the house from the Governor General.
Having been informed of the report that was to be made to the house I had a resolution prepared, and had it submitted to His Excellency the Governor General. I have it here now for consideration, and would be prepared at this time to deliver the Governor General's recommendation for consideration.
Of course this could not be dealt with, except by leave of the house, without 48 hours' notice. But if I have leave of the house I would be prepared to move that the house do, at its next sitting, resolve itself into a committee to consider the resolution.
